text: List the common complications after distal radius ORIF and the warning signs for each (EPL rupture, flexor tendon irritation/rupture, median neuropathy, stiffness, CRPS). Answer Key Acceptable reduction (distal radius): Radial height: within 2-3 mm of contralateral (~11 mm normal) Radial inclination: ≥ 15° (normal ~22°) Volar tilt: neutral to 10° dorsal acceptable (normal 11° volar); any dorsal angulation > 10° is concerning, especially in younger patients Articular step-off: ≤ 2 mm (some accept ≤ 1 mm for younger/active) DRUJ congruent Frykman uses two axes: intra-articular vs extra-articular (radiocarpal +/- DRUJ), and ulnar styloid involvement (yes/no). title: Session 3 — Tendon & Nerve Injuries
heading: Questions › Anatomy & classification
text: Name the 5 flexor tendon zones and state the single most important anatomic feature of each zone for repair. List the annular (A1-A5) and cruciate (C1-C3) pulleys, and identify which two pulleys are biomechanically most important to preserve. Classify jersey finger (Leddy). Which type needs repair within 7-10 days and why? Name the extensor tendon zones (Doyle) for the finger and the thumb. What is the classic injury at each even-numbered zone in the finger? title: Session 3 — Tendon & Nerve Injuries
heading: Questions › Board-style
text: The PRIMARY blood supply to the flexor tendons in the digit comes from: Intrinsic circulation within the tendon Vincula longa and brevia from the digital arteries The palmar arch Synovial diffusion alone A patient has a laceration at the wrist with loss of thumb opposition and loss of sensation over the palmar index and long fingers, but preserved wrist flexion and finger flexion. The most likely injured structure is: Median nerve at the wrist Anterior interosseous nerve Recurrent motor branch of median only Ulnar nerve at Guyon’s Answer Key See templates/flexor-tendon-repair-handout.md for in-depth answers on questions 1-3 and 9. Summary answers: Flexor zones: Zone I: only FDP (distal to FDS insertion on middle phalanx). Jersey finger territory. Zone II: “no man’s land” — A1 pulley to middle phalanx; both FDS + FDP in a narrow sheath under pulleys. Historically poor outcomes → Bunnell’s original injunction against primary repair; now primary repair is standard with early active motion. Zone III: palm (distal TCL edge to A1) — lumbrical origins; outcomes good. Zone IV: within the carpal tunnel — must protect median nerve, may need TCL release/repair. Zone V: forearm — often with nerve injuries; outcomes good if no nerve involvement. Pulleys: A1-A5 + C1-C3. A2 and A4 are biomechanically most important — venting one pulley partially is usually OK, but loss of both causes bowstringing. Modern teaching allows partial venting of A2 and A4 to facilitate repair. Leddy classification

heading: Questions › Board-style
text: The most sensitive provocative test for CTS is: Phalen’s Tinel’s at the wrist Durkan’s (carpal compression) Semmes-Weinstein monofilament The most common iatrogenic injury during an open carpal tunnel release is to the: Motor branch of median (recurrent) Palmar cutaneous branch of median Ulnar nerve at Guyon’s Superficial palmar arch Answer Key See ~/JanosClaude/templates/compressive-neuropathies-handout.md for detailed references. Summary answers: Carpal tunnel contents: 4 FDS + 4 FDP + 1 FPL + median nerve . heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020) › 4a. Mallet (Zone I — DIP) & Zone II (middle phalanx)
text: Phase Orthotic Exercises Precautions I — Immediate (day 1 to wk 6–8) DIP 10°–0° hyperextension. Tendinous mallet : 6–8 wk. Bony mallet : 6 wk. Op : 100% × 6 wk. Provide 2 splints (one for showering). Active PIP flex of affected finger with adjacent fingers held in extension. Daily skin check, DIP must stay extended. Consider taping DIP. If swan-neck → reduce passively, dorsal block PIP at 30°. II — Protective (wk 6 bony / wk 8 tendinous) Tendinous: orthosis 100% except exercise/hygiene. Bony: orthosis for strenuous activity + sleep × 2–4 wk. Remove orthotic. Gentle AROM DIP flex/ext: start 10° flex, progress 10° per week. Replace orthotic. Wk 8 : light activity out of orthosis if no lag. If DIP extensor lag ≥10° → orthosis 100% × 2–4 wk. III — Intermediate (wk 10) D/C during day. Night orthosis × 2 more wk. Fine motor, gradual flexion while maintaining DIP ext. Most zone 1–2 injuries finish with –10–0° extensor lag.

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020) › 4b. Boutonniere (Zone III — PIP)
text: Phase Orthotic Exercises Precautions I — Immediate (day 1 to wk 6) Orthosis or circumferential cast with PIP at 0°. Op: 100% × 6 wk. Active DIP flex of affected finger. If DIP hyperextension at wk 2 → reduce passively. II — Protective (wk 6) Convert to orthosis with PIP at 0°. Wk 7: reduce gradually as 0° PIP ext maintained. Light activity if no lag. Gentle active PIP ext to 30° flex, progress 10° per week. Replace orthotic. If PIP extensor lag ≥10° → orthosis 100% × 2–4 wk. III — Intermediate (wk 10) D/C. — —

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020) › 4c. Zones IV–VIII (proximal phalanx through forearm) — Immobilization Protocol
text: Week Orthotic Exercises Precautions 1–6 Volar digit static, PIP at absolute 0°, or serial cast. Lateral bands repaired → include DIP at 0°. Lateral bands intact → DIP free. ROM may start wk 3–6 depending on healing. AROM PIP flex to 30°, progress 10–20°/wk if no lag, 10 reps hourly. Lateral bands repaired → tendon gliding wk 3. Intact → wk 1. No forceful flex. No gripping. Splint between sessions. Serial cast if PIP contracture, closed injury, or noncompliant. 6–8 Wean from splint during day. Night splint continues. AAROM or dynamic flexion splint may start. Composite wrist + digit flex. Light functional use out of splint (≤1–3 lb). 10–12 D/C splint. PROM / PREs. —

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020) › 4d. Zones III–IV Alternative — Short Arc Motion (SAM) Protocol
text: Consider when broad tendon-bone interface in zone IV and adhesion risk is high. Week Orthotic Exercises Precautions 1 Digit volar immobilization: PIP & DIP at 0°, 24/7 except exercise. Two volar exercise splints: template 1 (PIP 30° flex, DIP 20° flex), template 2 (PIP 0°, DIP free). Remove immobilization hourly, AROM PIP & DIP, 10–20 reps in templates 1 & 2. Wrist held 30° flex, MP at 0°. Lateral bands repaired → limit DIP flex to 30–35° in template 2; intact → fully flex/extend DIP. PIP must be at 0° in immobilization splint to prevent extensor lag. 2 If no lag: progress template 1 → PIP 40–50°, DIP 30–40°. If extensor lag develops → smaller flex increments, focus on extension. If rupture suspected → MD. 3 If no lag: template 1 → PIP 50–60°, DIP 40–50°. — — 4 If no lag: template 1 → PIP 70–80°, DIP 50–60°. — If PIP stiff → intermittent splint into flex, continue static ext splint into wk 5–6. 5 Begin weaning. Composite flex and gentle PREs. Light functional activities out of splint. 6 D/C splint. Night PRN. PROM & PREs, reverse putty scraping. —

title: Tendon Repair Rehab — Resident Quick Reference
heading: 4. Primary Extensor — Hand & UE (2020) › 4e. Thumb Extensor (EPL) — Zones T1–T5 (BWH 2007)
text: Thumb zones differ from finger zones. EPL has its own zone map (T1–T5) and rehab protocols. Do not use finger zone I–VIII protocols for EPL repairs. Zone T1 (IP joint) — Immobilization Week Orthotic Exercises Precautions 1–3 IP at 0° or slight hyperextension, continuously. Op : 5–6 wk. Non-op : 8 wk. Provide 2nd splint for showers. None. No IP flexion. No gripping or pinching in splint. McConnell tape to hold digit during splint changes. 5–6 Op: remove for exercise, otherwise continuously ×2–4 more wk. Op : AROM IP flex in 20° increments/wk, modifying if extensor lag develops, 10 reps hourly. Non-op : no ROM yet. If extensor lag ≥10° → continuous splint ×2–4 wk, reassess. 8 Gradually wean during day. Continue at night. Op : AAROM if needed, provided no extensor lag. Non-op : initiate AROM IP flex in 20° increments. — 10–12 D/C splint. Op : PROM, PREs (light grip/pinch). Non-op : AAROM → PROM → PREs as tolerated. — Zone T2 (proximal phalanx) — Immobilization Week Orthotic Exercises Precautions 1 Hand-based static splint (short opponens): MP and IP at 0°, thumb in radial abduction. None. No active motion. 3 Same. Initiate AROM flexion at each joint; progress 25–30°/wk. Tendon-to-bone adherence may limit excursion in this zone. 4–5 Same. AAROM flexion, isolated and combined joint. Light prehension ADL out of splint. — 6 Begin to wean. Dynamic flexion splinting PRN. Moderate prehension ADL out of splint. — 8 D/C splint. PREs. Full function. — Zones T3–T4 (MP joint / metacarpal) —

heading: 2. Flexor (FDS + FDP) — Modified Duran · Zones 1–5
text: Use when EAM is deferred. Same orthotic, exercises are passive only in Phase I. Phase Orthotic Exercises Precautions I — Immediate (day 3 to wk 2) Same as EAM (zones 1–3 vs 4–5). Active non-resistive thumb flex with wrist ext. Light prehensile in therapy. 5 D/C orthosis. Gentle blocking for thumb IP flex. — 6 Dynamic IP ext splinting PRN. Putty scraping PRN. May start NMES/US PRN. — 8 — Gradually add resistive exercises. —

heading: Key principles
text: Repair is weakest day 5–21 . Strong repair (4-strand core + epitendinous) is the prerequisite for EAM. Adhesions favor extrinsic healing; controlled motion favors intrinsic healing. Gap >3 mm → ↑ rupture and adhesion risk. Always cross-check with surgeon’s op note (suture configuration, pulley/nerve/vessel work).

heading: Red flags at follow-up
text: Sudden loss of active flexion / extension after gain → assume rupture. Refer to surgeon. Extensor lag ≥10° → return to full-time orthosis × 2–4 weeks. PIP contracture developing → serial casting or static progressive splint, escalate therapy. No improvement in tendon glide after 6–8 weeks → discuss tenolysis (typically deferred to ≥3–6 months post-op). Persistent edema beyond 4 weeks → edema control, rule out infection.

title: Hand Infections
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Most infections superficial (skin/SC); most common site: dorsal subcutaneous tissues Frequency: paronychia (35%), cellulitis (35%), felons (15%), flexor sheath (10%), deep space (2%), septic arthritis (2%), osteomyelitis (1%) Most common organisms: S. aureus + beta-hemolytic strep ; MRSA: 34-73% of hand infections Small finger + thumb flexor sheaths extend to ulnar/radial bursae in 32-80% Anatomic variations of the digital flexor sheaths and radial/ulnar bursae, with relative frequency. title: Hand Infections
heading: Specific Infections › Animal Bites
text: Cat bites: 30-50% infection rate (vs 15% dog); Pasteurella multocida most common isolate Empiric: amox/clav PO or amp/sulbactam IV Cat bites: NEVER close primarily. Extend the puncture, formal I&D, debride, and pack open . Closing a cat bite traps inoculated Pasteurella in a deep narrow puncture that re-seals over the inoculum. Dog bites: loose primary closure acceptable after adequate debridement Barrera: Cat bites — never close. Extend and pack open. Dog bites — loose closure after debridement is fine. The cat bite is a needle-thin puncture that inoculates deep and re-seals over Pasteurella; closing it manufactures a fulminant infection.

title: Hand Infections
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: What are Kanavel’s 4 signs of pyogenic flexor tenosynovitis? — A: Fusiform swelling, flexed posture, pain on passive extension, tenderness along flexor tendon sheath. Q: A patient presents with a tense, throbbing fingertip with erythema after a puncture wound. Swelling does NOT extend proximal to the DIP crease. What is the diagnosis and preferred surgical approach? — A: Felon; longitudinal incision over pulp at maximal fluctuance (or distal lateral mid-axial on non-border side), bluntly disrupting septae. Q: What organism in leech saliva requires prophylactic antibiotics during leech therapy, and what is the characteristic organism in human bite infections? — A: Aeromonas hydrophila (leeches); Eikenella corrodens (human bites, though S. aureus and Group A Strep are more common). Q: What is the LRINEC score threshold that has a 92% PPV for necrotizing fasciitis? — A: Score >6 (components: CRP, WBC, hemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose). Q: A patient with chronic paronychia for 3 months has thickened, ridged nails and tender red nail folds. What is the most likely organism? — A: Candida albicans (present in 40-95% of chronic paronychia cases).

title: Hand Infections
heading: Specific Infections › Felon

title: Hand Infections
heading: Specific Infections › Necrotizing Fasciitis
text: Surgical emergency ; progresses from cellulitis-like → crepitus, nonpitting edema, hypotension Type 1 : mixed aerobic/anaerobic (immunocompromised); Type 2 : Group A Strep/Staph (extremities) LRINEC score >6: PPV 92% (CRP, WBC, Hgb, Na, Cr, glucose) Empiric: ampicillin-sulbactam + clindamycin + ciprofloxacin ; urgent debridement of all necrotic tissue Mortality: 23-76% ; DM most common comorbidity; delay >24h → higher mortality

title: Hand Infections
heading: Specific Infections › Paronychia
text: Acute (<6 wk) : S. aureus most common; warm soaks + PO abx if early; abscess → elevate nail fold or incise; point blade away from germinal matrix ; complete nail removal if entire plate undermined Chronic (>6 wk) : Candida albicans 40-95% ; Beau’s lines; topical antifungal or systemic azole; topical corticosteroids: 87.5% improvement ; surgical marsupialization if refractory Paronychia decompression — slide the scalpel between the nail plate and nail fold to enter the abscess, blade pointed away from the germinal matrix. title: Hand Infections
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: MRSA is 34-73% of hand infections — empiric coverage is mandatory Herpetic whitlow: NEVER incise — self-limited; incision risks devastating complications Kanavel’s signs are only 54% sensitive — low threshold for surgical exploration “Fusiform” swelling is a misnomer — lateral XR volar−dorsal soft tissue at P1 ≥ 7 mm shifts probability sharply toward PFT CRP is the most useful lab for flexor tenosynovitis (76% sensitivity) Fight bites: always explore the MCP joint — even if wound appears superficial Cat bites infect twice as often as dog bites — and must NEVER be closed primarily Crystals do NOT exclude septic arthritis — always culture Empiric abx for hand septic arthritis is vanc + Unasyn (or Zosyn), not vanc + TMP-SMX (double MRSA coverage) LRINEC >6 for necrotizing fasciitis: this score can be life-saving

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Board-Style Questions

Q: What is the watershed line and why does it matter? A: Distal-most ridge of volar radius; plate placement distal to it predisposes to flexor tendon rupture (esp FPL, index FDP). Q: When is ulnar styloid fixation indicated after volar plate ORIF of distal radius? A: Only when clinical DRUJ instability after radius fixation; routine styloid fixation not needed. Q: What’s the most reliable radiographic predictor of DRUJ instability? A: Coronal plane shift of the distal radius (not ulnar styloid fracture presence).

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › Distal Ulna
text: Reduced + aligned ulna can heal without internal fixation when radius stable on volar plate Unstable displaced ulnar head/neck → 2.0-2.4 mm plate (ulnar or volar position) Preserve ulnar head; resection = salvage

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › DRUJ Management
text: Examine contralateral side preop AND in OR after radius fixation Ulnar styloid fixation NOT routine after volar plate ORIF unless clinical DRUJ instability Options if unstable: foveal TFCC repair, ulnar styloid ORIF (hook plate / tension band), DRUJ cross-pinning, supination/neutral splinting If cross-pinning DRUJ: 0.062” K-wires, 4 cortices, neutral rotation, exit pin both sides of skin so a broken pin can still be retrieved

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Open wound near apex of deformity Acute CTS vs nerve contusion : contusion = immediate fixed deficit; acute CTS = evolving pain + paresthesia DRUJ stability check: always compare with contralateral side (clinic + preop)

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: AP, lateral, oblique — measure ulnar variance, radial inclination (22°), volar tilt (11°), sigmoid notch obliquity Volar teardrop angle (Medoff) — confirms volar lunate facet reduction CT after reduction for articular or distal displaced fractures + comminution + associated carpal fractures

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › Initial — All Fractures
text: Hematoma block with 1% lidocaine (rapid onset, resolves for post-reduction exam) Traction 8-10 lb with finger traps; palmar translation of neutral lunate is key Padded 3-point molded sugar-tong splint, wrist neutral One concerted reduction attempt; repeated manipulation causes harm without benefit in elderly

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Complications & Outcomes › Major Complications
text: Acute CTS — urgent release (distinguish from contusion — contusion is non-progressive) EPL rupture — most common after nonop, esp minimally displaced; treat with EIP-to-EPL transfer Flexor tendon rupture (FPL, index FDP) — too-distal volar plate (past watershed); use US to monitor (small plate-to-tendon ratio = urgent removal) Malunion — radial shortening + dorsal angulation most common Nonunion — rare; workup metabolic/mechanical/infection; vitamin D , smoking cessation CRPS 3-10% — aggressive rehab, neuropathic meds, sympathetic blocks, CTR Ligament injuries : SL 4.7-46%, LT 12-34%, TFCC 39-82% (peripheral with ulnar styloid usually doesn’t need repair)

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Cast 3-4 wk → removable splint by wk 4 if alignment stable Pad DRSN + DUCN; avoid extreme flexion; ensure digital ROM Weekly films first 3-4 wk Elderly low-demand patient: gentle attempt at reduction acceptable; deformity well tolerated Combined distal radius + ulna fracture in elderly → consider surgery (loss of strut → significant deformity/nonunion)

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: Volar (FCR) Approach — Workhorse 8 cm incision over FCR Protect LABC nerve (radial), PCBM nerve (ulnar; may travel within FCR sheath or superficial — inspect fat carefully) Release distal BR insertion to reduce deforming force PQ released radially + distally Extended FCR (Orbay) : best visualization of volar ulnar corner Plate proximal to watershed line; distal pegs 75% of volar-dorsal distance Intraop fluoro views: AP, lateral, tilt views (10° lunate, 30° scaphoid), pronated + supinated oblique, dorsal tangential, near-axial sigmoid Subtract 1-2 mm from drill measurement to avoid dorsal prominence Dorsal Midline For complex articular fractures requiring direct joint visualization Protect SBRN + SBUN; 3rd compartment incision to retract EPL (transpose at closure) PIN neurectomy + ligament-sparing capsulotomy 2.0-2.4 mm dorsal plates; low profile, subperiosteal Fragment-Specific (Medoff) Multiple small plates form fixed-angle triangular constructs (plate proximal screws + K-wire through distal hole into opposite cortex) Excellent for highly comminuted; orthogonal plating common External Fixator / Dorsal Bridge Plate Severe comminution, soft tissue compromise, polytrauma needing weight bearing Index MC pins (2.5 mm Shanz; first at metaphyseal flare, second distal parallel) Radius pins through ECRL/ECRB interval (bare area, 4 fingerbreadths proximal to styloid) Check extrinsic tightness at end (passive IP flexion shouldn’t extend MCPs = no over-distraction) Bridge plate removed

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Complications & Outcomes › Outcomes (RCTs)
text: Surgical vs non-op in > 65 yo : better radiographs with surgery, similar function at 1 yr, more complications with surgery Pinning vs ex-fix : no difference Volar plate vs pinning : better DASH at 3 mo, equal at 1 yr Bridging vs non-bridging ex-fix : McQueen showed non-bridging better; later studies equivocal AAOS CPG : unable to recommend one technique over another

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Don’t miss volar marginal fragment — primary indication for ulnar-side approach (between flexor tendons + FCU) Coronal shift must be corrected to restore sigmoid notch + DRUJ tension BR tendon release dramatically reduces deforming force Hardware too distal (within 3 mm of volar lip) = flexor rupture risk Watch for prominent dorsal screws — Lister tubercle blocks them on standard lateral; use dorsal tangential view Younger active patients benefit most from surgery; very low-demand elderly accept deformity well Combined distal radius + ulna fracture in elderly = consider surgery despite age (loss of strut → high deformity + nonunion risk)

title: Distal Radius and Ulna Fractures
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Volar plate: protected wrist motion + grip strengthening early External fixator removed ~6 wk in clinic Bridge plate at ~3 mo Maximum recovery 6-12 mo from injury

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Most frequently fractured carpal bone ; high nonunion risk 3 reasons for nonunion: no cambium layer (no periosteal callus), flexion/humpback force, retrograde blood supply Blood supply (Gelberman): 2 pedicles off radial artery Distal pole pedicle → tubercle → supplies distal 20-30% Dorsal ridge vessels → enter at/distal to waist → supply proximal 70-80% No intraosseous anastomoses between the two Proximal pole fracture nonunion rate 34% non-op (Eastley meta-analysis) Distribution: waist 65%, distal pole 25%, proximal pole 10%

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What’s the nonunion rate for proximal pole scaphoid fractures treated non-operatively? A: 34% (Eastley meta-analysis) — operative fixation is standard. Q: Which fluoro views are required during scaphoid ORIF? A: AP, AP with ulnar deviation, lateral, semipronated, semisupinated. Q: Per the Buijze RCT, what is the optimal cast type for non-/minimally displaced waist fractures? A: Short-arm cast, thumb free, 10 weeks. Q: What does the SWIFFT RCT show about surgery vs cast for waist fractures < 2 mm displaced? A: No PRWE difference at 52 weeks; surgery faster at 12 weeks but more complications. Q: Why is the proximal pole at highest risk for AVN? A: Retrograde dorsal ridge vessel supply; no intraosseous anastomosis with distal pedicle.

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Classification
text: Mayo / Herbert / Russe — none reliably predict nonunion Most useful in practice: location (proximal, waist, distal) + displacement (CT) Unstable (Mayo): displacement > 1 mm, DISI, capitolunate > 15°, SL angle > 60°, lateral intrascaphoid > 35°, comminuted, perilunate Arthroscopic probing > imaging for true instability (Buijze)

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Complication Avoidance Nonunion Right treatment for right fracture; smoking cessation Humpback malunion Early fixation for at-risk fractures Hardware prominence 5-view fluoro; common reason for reop CRPS, nerve, infection Soft tissue handling, abx prophylaxis SWIFFT RCT (Dias 2020): 408 waist fractures < 2 mm — no PRWE difference at 52 wk between surgery + cast; surgery faster at 12 wk but more complications (nerve, CRPS, infection) Surgery: faster RTW, sometimes better grip/ROM (longer casts in non-op groups confound) Heavy laborers: 7-week RTW benefit with surgery (Majeed)

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Snuffbox tenderness + scaphoid tubercle tenderness Pain with ulnar deviation = only finding predictive of true fracture (ML study)

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: Plain films: PA, lateral, scaphoid view (PA, ulnar deviation, 45° pronation) Plain x-rays miss occult fractures — 13% missed even on follow-up MRI ~100% sensitive for occult fracture; also assesses AVN (though AVN doesn’t predict union outcomes — Rancy) CT = lower sensitivity, excellent specificity; best for displacement, location, comminution Meta-analysis: immediate CT or MRI most cost-effective strategy

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Indications: tubercle, non/minimally displaced distal pole, non/minimally displaced waist fractures Standard: short-arm cast, thumb-free × 10 wk (Buijze RCT) — long-arm and thumb-spica do not improve outcomes Union 98% in CT-confirmed minimally displaced waist (Buijze) Average time to union: distal 53d, waist 65d, proximal 113d (Grewal) Check CT at 6-8 wk to confirm bone bridging — clinical exam unreliable since not all nonunions are painful

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: Indications Displacement > 2 mm Humpback deformity All proximal pole fractures Fracture-dislocations / concomitant DR fracture Relative: comminution, delayed presentation (> 4 wk), patients needing faster RTW Fixation Single headless compression screw, central in scaphoid axis, as long as possible without joint penetration (Dodds) Double-screw constructs only in high-demand athletes (↑ biomechanical strength but ↑ vascular + hardware risk) Volar buttress plating for waist comminution / persistent humpback (frequent removal) Approach by location Proximal pole → dorsal (antegrade) Mini-open: 1 cm distal + slight ulnar to Lister tubercle, transverse capsulotomy, wrist flexed, guidewire across fracture Subtract 4-6 mm from measured length (avoid distraction, ensure subchondral seating) Waist + distal pole → volar (retrograde) Hockey-stick incision over FCR, identify + protect superficial radial artery branch Resect portion of volar trapezium for proper screw start DISI correction: temporary K-wire from radius into lunate at neutral, then extend wrist K-wire derotation if needed Arthroscopic-assisted (Geissler, Wong): allows direct visualization of reduction + assesses concomitant ligament injuries (Jørgsholm: high incidence) Intraop fluoro views: AP, AP ulnar deviation, lateral, semipronated, semisupinated — all 5 to confirm screw centrality and avoid joint penetration

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Snuffbox + tubercle tenderness with negative x-ray → straight to MRI (most cost-effective) AVN on MRI does NOT predict union outcomes — don’t let it drive surgical decisions Don’t trust radiographic “union” — CT for bone bridging Central screw placement matters more than length 5 fluoro views during ORIF, period Many “unstable” Herbert B fractures are stable on arthroscopic probing

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Pediatric Pearls
text: Scaphoid = most common pediatric carpal fracture (0.45% of all peds fx); peak age ~15 yo Ossifies last (~age 5 M / 4 F at distal pole, progresses proximally) Waist 68% > distal 27% > proximal 6% in open physes; proximal % rises with maturity 28-37% present as nonunions (athletes minimize symptoms) MRI > CT (avoid pediatric ionizing radiation) Acute nondisplaced: 90-99% heal in cast Displaced waist/distal: 20-30% heal in cast → ORIF recommended Proximal pole or small ossific nucleus → consider two 1.1 mm K-wires instead of screw to protect blood supply

title: Scaphoid Fractures
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Short-arm thumb spica until CT shows > 50% bone bridging (typically 6-12 wk) Athletes: cleared at > 50% bridging + restored ROM; average RTW 7.3 wk post-op (vs 13.9 wk post-cast removal in non-op) — systematic review: 98% return post-op vs 90% non-op Cast immobilization during play not recommended (significant nonunion risk)

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Overall scaphoid fracture nonunion rate ~15% ; proximal pole fractures nonunite at ~34% without operative fixation (Eastley meta-analysis — matches FX-02). Once a proximal pole nonunion is established, persistent nonunion despite open grafting + fixation = up to ~68% (Ramamurthy 2007) — drives the case for early definitive ORIF rather than salvage grafting later. 97% of untreated nonunions → SNAC (Mack, Ruby, Inoue) Retrograde blood supply via dorsal ridge perforators from radial artery; minor volar tubercle supply from superficial palmar branch RSC ligament = fulcrum for humpback deformity at waist nonunion 75% of scaphoid covered in cartilage ; dorsal ridge = non-articular bone (osteophyte/impingement site) Dorsal ridge osteophytes → loss of wrist extension (classic clinical sign of waist nonunion)

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › Approach by Location
text: Waist with humpback → volar (FCR extended) + structural graft + retrograde or antegrade screw Proximal pole → dorsal + cancellous or vascularized inlay + antegrade screw Distal pole → volar

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › Arthroscopic Repair (Oh, Slade)
text: Comparable union + functional outcomes vs open Preserves extrinsic ligaments + capsular vascularity Best for fibrous nonunions or those without humpback/bone loss

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Biomechanics
text: Untreated waist nonunion: distal pole flexes + pronates + ulnar deviates ; proximal pole + lunate extend = DISI pattern Oka 3D CT: nonunions distal to dorsal SL fibers → 36° proximal extension + 19° supination, lunate 18° + 6°, triquetrum 12° + 3°, dorsal translation 3.1 mm scaphoid + 2.6 mm capitate Proximal pole nonunions = no humpback (proximal to dorsal SL fibers → distal pole doesn’t flex) Amadio: lateral intrascaphoid angle > 45° → 54% DJD

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What’s the rate of persistent nonunion after operative grafting + fixation for an established proximal pole scaphoid nonunion? A: ~68% (Ramamurthy 2007) — drives the case for early definitive ORIF when the fracture is still fresh, rather than salvaging the nonunion later. Q: Why is a volar wedge graft preferred over dorsal inlay for waist nonunion with humpback? A: Volar wedge provides structural support against flexion deformity; dorsal inlay doesn’t and tends to fail. Q: What four factors predict failure of scaphoid nonunion surgery (Nakamura)? A: > 5 yr from injury, proximal pole, proximal sclerosis, poor scaphoid/carpal reduction. Q: Which vascularized graft uses the descending genicular artery and has the highest union rate? A: Medial femoral condyle (MFC) free flap — Aibinder reported 89% at 16 wk. Q: What two adjunctive procedures stabilize the scaphoid against humpback flexion forces? A: Volar scaphoid plate (Dodds) and scaphocapitate pinning/screw.

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › Bone Graft Options
text: Non-vascularized (workhorse) Cancellous from distal radius (local; ideal — backfill donor with allograft/substitute to prevent fracture) Corticocancellous wedge (Russe/Fernandez) for humpback Iliac crest if larger structural graft needed Vascularized Pedicled Flap Pedicle Use 1,2 ICSRA (Zaidemberg) Branch between 1st and 2nd compartments Proximal pole or rotated volar for waist (with limited styloidectomy < 5-6 mm) Volar carpal artery Distal edge of PQ from radial artery Volar wedge for waist humpback Dorsal capsular (Sotereanos) Capsule-based, posterior interosseous extension Proximal pole , esp with AVN; robust hardy pedicle, no specific artery dissection Free Vascularized MFC / MFT — descending genicular artery (DGA) off SFA MFT mimics proximal pole curvature (osteochondral) Doi: 100% union for waist nonunion with humpback Aibinder: MFC 89% union at 16 wk vs 1,2 ICSRA 79% at 26 wk vs iliac crest 71% at 19 wk

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Classification
text: By location: distal pole, waist , proximal pole — drives surgical approach + graft type By chronicity: fibrous (nascent) → established nonunion with sclerosis/cysts By deformity: humpback present/absent Nakamura 4 failure predictors : > 5 years from injury, proximal pole, proximal sclerosis, poor scaphoid/carpal reduction

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Persistent nonunion, infection, hardware failure, CRPS, progression to SNAC Slade : treatment within 6 mo of original injury = significantly higher union (minimal bone loss/sclerosis) Fernandez: 30/37 with mild-moderate DJD at 6 yr after wedge graft, but none progressed to SNAC after union Pinder systematic review (48 studies, 1,602 pts): no statistical difference : Screws 88%, K-wires 92%, no internal fixation 79% union Sample sizes underpowered — would need 3,400 patients for 80% power Alluri vascularized graft meta-analysis: 92% complete satisfaction, MMWS + DASH improved 53% + 82%

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › Contraindications (relative)
text: Significant medical comorbidities, uncontrolled CRPS, fixed carpal malalignment, advanced SNAC, asymptomatic radiographic malunion in low-demand patient Active smoking

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › Dorsal Approach
text: Longitudinal incision, just distal + ulnar to Lister Release EPL; retract 4th compartment ulnarly Berger ligament-sparing capsulotomy Wrist flexion exposes proximal pole Limit distal dissection to preserve dorsal capsular blood supply Use wider reamer or “micro” screw for tenuous proximal pole (avoid comminution)

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Loss of wrist extension; pain doing push-ups; snuff box + volar tubercle tenderness Watson shift; midcarpal instability with forced ulnar deviation Giugale : wrist extension increases palpable volar scaphoid surface area 168% Mallee meta-analysis: snuff box sens 0.87-1.00; Parvizi combined tests → spec 74%, sens 100%

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › Fixation Options
text: Headless compression screw (gold standard); 4 steps: guidewire → measure → ream → insert Two screws for additional bending stability (Garcia) Scaphocapitate K-wire (0.062”) or screw to block midcarpal flexion forces Volar scaphoid plate (Dodds) — for recalcitrant nonunions, buttress against flexion, supports volar wedge graft

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: AP, lateral, oblique, navicular (AP ulnar deviation) CT in scaphoid long axis (sagittal reformat) = standard preop: Precise location Bone loss + cystic erosions Deformity (lateral intrascaphoid angle, height-to-length) Sclerosis of proximal pole MRI : T1 dark marrow = AVN; Rancy challenges whether AVN actually impacts outcomes 50% bridging trabeculae on CT = healed (Guss) 16-27% of scaphoid fractures have normal initial radiographs

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › Indications
text: Active symptomatic patient with confirmed nonunion Humpback deformity, bone loss, prior failed surgery, AVN

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › NOT Recommended
text: BMP-2/OP-1 abandoned — Brannan: unacceptably high HO + wrist stiffness rates Dorsal inlay graft for humpback (no structural support → failure)

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Volar wedge graft for humpback; dorsal inlay graft for proximal pole — match graft to deformity Don’t reduce screw → fragment small proximal pole; use wider reamer or micro screw AVN on MRI does NOT predict outcome (Rancy) — don’t let it drive decision BMP-2 = avoid Limited radial styloidectomy < 5-6 mm preserves RSC ligament Treat early — < 6 mo from injury has highest union rate For chronic nonunion with isolated radioscaphoid arthrosis, distal pole excision is a low-morbidity salvage

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Short-arm orthosis 10-14 d Cast extension to 6 wk total common CT at ~3 mo for ≥ 50% bridging before RTW heavy lifting / RTP for athletes Scaphoid heals by direct bone healing (intrasynovial bone) — minimal callus

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › Salvage
text: Distal scaphoid pole excision (Malerich): 17/19 favorable at 15 yr — good option in chronic nonunion with radioscaphoid arthrosis

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › Surgical Planning Imaging
text: Preop CT in scaphoid long axis is mandatory — defines location, bone loss, deformity, sclerosis Intraop fluoro views: AP, AP+UD, lateral, semipronated, semisupinated

title: Scaphoid Nonunion
heading: Treatment › Volar Approach
text: FCR-radial artery interval; preserve RSC ligament insertion on proximal pole Debride to healthy bone; reduce with ulnar deviation + distal pole supination Laminar spreader for severe bone loss Provisional fixation: central guidewire ± K-wires capturing both poles; pin proximal pole to lunate / distal to capitate

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Triquetrum › Anatomy
text: > 90% are dorsal cortical (chip) fractures Avulsion of dorsal radiocarpal + dorsal intercarpal ligaments; or direct impact

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Trapezium › Anatomy
text: Saddle-shaped articulation with thumb MC TCL attachment + FCR groove Body fractures: sagittal split, horizontal split, transarticular, dorsoradial tuberosity, comminuted Volar ridge: type I (base), type II (tip avulsion) Mechanism: axial load on dorsiflexed wrist (thumb MC driven into trapezium) Can occur with Bennett fracture

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Capitate › Anatomy
text: 1-2% of carpal fractures Central pillar of wrist; articulates with lunate + scaphoid proximally Historically thought tenuous proximal blood supply (retrograde) but Kadar micro-CT: 70% have proximal vessel → AVN less common than predicted

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Lunate › Anatomy
text: Primary axial load transmitter to radiocarpal joint Fractures < 1% of carpal — distinct from Kienböck AVN

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Trapezoid › Anatomy
text: Base of 2nd MC; isolated fracture rare; usually with other injuries Most missed carpal injury — Kain: only 5/11 initially recognized; coronal patterns visible only on CT

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Pisiform › Anatomy
text: Sesamoid in FCU; pisotriquetral joint 0.5-2% of carpal fractures; sports-related (direct blow, repetitive) Pediatric: multiple ossification centers (CT confirms vs fracture)

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: 8 carpal bones : proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum); distal row (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate) Pisiform = sesamoid in FCU tendon; pisotriquetral joint; not part of mechanical proximal row Frequency of carpal fractures (excl scaphoid) : Triquetrum 18% (most common after scaphoid) Hamate 5% Trapezium 1-5% Capitate 1-2% Lunate < 1% Trapezoid + pisiform 0.5-2% (rare)

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What sports are classically associated with hook of hamate fractures and what’s the standard treatment? A: Racket sports, baseball, golf; excision of the fragment for symptomatic nonunion (preferred over ORIF for most athletes). Q: What is scaphocapitate (Fenton’s) syndrome? A: Transcaphoid perilunate dislocation with capitate head rotated 90-180° in sagittal plane; requires operative reduction. Q: A proximal radial corner triquetrum fracture on PA radiograph should make you suspect what? A: Perilunate instability / LT ligament injury / VISI deformity. Q: What is the most commonly missed carpal fracture and what imaging confirms it? A: Trapezoid fracture; CT (coronal patterns are invisible on plain films). Q: Which nerve branch is at greatest risk during hook of hamate excision? A: Motor branch of the ulnar nerve as it dives deep around the distal-ulnar aspect of the hook.

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Missed injury → nonunion, persistent pain, secondary arthrosis Hook of hamate nonunion → FDP attrition/rupture, ulnar neuropathy Capitate AVN concerns historically overstated; rare in practice Trapezoid + capitate fractures (when missed) → midcarpal arthritis Pisiform: post-traumatic pisotriquetral arthrosis if untreated nonunion

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Hamate › Dorsal Hamate Fracture with CMC Dislocation
text: 4th + 5th CMC fracture-dislocation = surgical Cain classification of hamato-MC fracture-dislocations Compression screw or K-wire to restore congruency; cross-pin to adjacent stable MC or scaphoid body if fragment too small Athletes with persistent hypothenar pain after “wrist sprain” — get a carpal tunnel view or CT to rule out hook fracture; excision is the standard operation

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Hamate › Hook of Hamate
text: Classic in racket sports, baseball, golf (butt of club/bat impacts hypothenar) Adjacent to ulnar NV bundle; attachment for TCL Nonunion → flexor tendon attrition (esp ulnar digits), ulnar neuropathy Treatment Nonop trial OK with early recognition: thumb-spica cast (minimize TCL pulling force) Hirano: 2/5 cast-treated → nonunion needing surgery Symptomatic nonunion → excision (gold standard) Approach: volar incision over hook; protect motor branch of ulnar nerve (dives deep around distal-ulnar hook); release hypothenar attachments Smooth bone base after excision Most athletes return to play promptly post-excision (Devers) ORIF (Watson) and ultrasound bone stimulator alternatives — limited evidence

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Triquetrum dorsal chip = stable, splint for comfort — but proximal radial corner = perilunate marker Hook of hamate — get carpal tunnel view + CT, excise if symptomatic Always image opposite wrist for pediatric pisiform (ossification variation vs fracture) Scaphocapitate syndrome = look for rotated capitate head in perilunate injury Capitate AVN concerns historically overstated — recent CT data shows reliable proximal supply Trapezoid fractures need CT — easily missed coronal split pattern Volar ridge trapezium fractures often misdiagnosed as contusion

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Hook of hamate excision: short cast for comfort × 1 wk → motion Lunate ORIF: 4-6 wk SAC; CT at 8-12 wk to confirm healing Capitate ORIF: 4-6 wk cast → motion Athletes (post-hook excision): typically RTP by 6-8 wk

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Capitate › Scaphocapitate Syndrome (Fenton’s)
text: Transcaphoid perilunate dislocation + capitate head rotated 90-180° sagittal plane Easily missed on x-ray Operative reduction mandatory — missed → nonunion + midcarpal arthritis

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Triquetrum › Treatment
text: Nonoperative : cast/orthosis based on pain — mainstay High rate of dorsal ligament injury on MRI (Becce) — but does not correlate with bone marrow edema or change management Concomitant TFCC injury can cause persistent ulnar-side pain (Lee) Proximal radial corner triquetrum fracture (near LT) on PA = marker for perilunate instability / LT injury / VISI — surgical stabilization warranted

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Trapezium › Treatment
text: Nonop: thumb spica × 4-6 wk for non-displaced Displaced body / joint incongruity → ORIF (compression screw, K-wire, or ex-fix/dynamic traction for comminution) Volar ridge fractures: often missed, treated as contusion; symptomatic nonunion → excision

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Capitate › Treatment

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Lunate › Treatment
text: Non-displaced dorsal/chip: cast 1 wk + weekly reexam (rule out missed concomitant injury) Volar body fracture → extended carpal tunnel approach , headless compression screw Small avulsion with ligamentous injury → suture anchor; K-wire SL + LT stabilization Pin scaphoid-capitate to prevent proximal capitate migration compressing lunate Body fractures with intra-articular extension → dorsal approach between 3rd + 4th compartments Perilunate-associated lunate fractures: pinning if fragments too small for screw

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Trapezoid › Treatment

title: Carpal Fractures (Non-Scaphoid)
heading: Pisiform › Treatment

title: Metacarpal Fractures
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Physes: distal end for index-long-ring-small MC; thumb MC physis at PROXIMAL end (occasional pseudophysis distally) Vascular: nutrient artery to diaphysis middle third Thumb + index: ulnar aspect Long, ring, small: radial aspect MC head: epiphyseal arteriole + collateral ligament association; arteriole absent in 35% → pericapsular dependence (AVN risk) MC head cam-shaped — palmar diameter > dorsal → collaterals tight in flexion (intrinsic-plus position protects) Shortening 2 mm → 7° extensor lag + 8% intrinsic loss ; 10 mm → 50% intrinsic power loss Border MCs (thumb, index, small) more prone to shortening 1° MC malrotation = 5° finger malrotation — poorly tolerated

title: Metacarpal Fractures
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What is the Jahss maneuver? A: MCP + PIP flexed 90°, dorsally directed pressure on PIP, volar pressure on MC shaft to reduce a metacarpal neck fracture. Q: Per the Martínez-Catalán study, how should an isolated 5th MC neck fracture with < 70° angulation and no rotation be treated? A: Soft wrap + buddy taping (non-inferior to reduction + casting; faster RTW). Q: What is the impact of plate position near MCP/CMC on hardware removal rate (Grisdela)? A: 50% removal if within 1 cm of MCP; 30% if within 0.5 cm of CMC. Q: Why is MC malrotation poorly tolerated? A: 1° of MC malrotation produces 5° of finger malrotation, causing scissoring and functional loss. Q: What is the suspected diagnosis when a dorsal hamate rim fracture is seen? A: 4th/5th CMC fracture-dislocation — get CT.

title: Metacarpal Fractures
heading: MC Neck Fractures › Boxer’s Fracture (5th MC neck)
text: Young adult males; direct axial blow Apex dorsal deformity (intrinsic pull on distal fragment) Always check rotation — never accept any malrotation Barrera: boxer’s fracture < 70° angulation with no malrotation → buddy tape, no reduction.

title: Metacarpal Fractures
heading: MC Shaft Fractures › Closed Reduction
text: Hematoma block (1% lidocaine) 3-point mold: dorsal at apex, volar prox + dist PIPs free; recheck at 1 wk → cast 2 wk → brace total 6 wk

title: Metacarpal Fractures
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Stiffness = most common complication Malunion, nonunion, hardware failure, infection, NV injury Tendon adhesions (plate > screw) Dorsal ulnar sensory nerve injury (esp 5th MC pin) Open fracture: low infection rate even > 12 hr (Tulipan) — debride when soft tissue OK; not emergent unless contaminated

title: Metacarpal Fractures
heading: MC Shaft Fractures › CRPP (Percutaneous Pinning)
text: Acute, minimal exposure, fewer adhesions Configurations: retrograde, antegrade IM, transverse to adjacent MC Galal RCT (transverse vs IM, 5th MC neck > 30°): Equivalent outcomes Transverse faster (10 vs 32 min) IM higher complications (backout, infection, dorsal ulnar sensory injury) Buried K-wires < infection than exposed

title: Metacarpal Fractures
heading: Workup › Exam

title: Metacarpal Fractures
heading: MC Shaft Fractures › External Fixation
text: Severe comminution, soft tissue, contamination, bone loss 2× 2.0 mm half pins; 45° dorsal-ulnar or dorsal-radial avoids extensors Bone grafting (iliac crest corticocancellous) or Masquelet induced membrane (2-stage) for segmental loss When plate position is close to a joint, counsel patient about high removal rate: 50% within 1 cm of MCP, 30% within 0.5 cm of CMC (Grisdela)

title: Metacarpal Fractures
heading: MC Shaft Fractures › Headless Compression Screws (IM antegrade)
text: Hug systematic review (693 MC + 265 phalangeal): 100% union at 5.7 wk, 3.2% complications, DASH 3.7, TAM 243° Supichyangur RCT: HCS RTW at 3 wk, better early ROM vs K-wire Technique: sagittal band split, dorsal capsulotomy, entry at dorsal one-third MC head, cannulated drill, HCS Avery cadaver: single IM screw > 2 retrograde K-wires Long-term arthritis risk at insertion unknown — small cartilage footprint documented

title: Thumb Fractures + Ligament Injuries
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What deforming force on the distal Bennett fragment causes its dorsal/proximal/radial subluxation? A: Abductor pollicis longus (APL). Q: What is a Stener lesion? A: Complete UCL rupture with retraction and interposition of the adductor pollicis aponeurosis — blocks healing, surgical indication. Q: What angle of laxity on valgus stress confirms thumb MCP UCL instability? A: > 35° absolute or > 15° more than contralateral. Q: What is the prognostic significance of articular step-off in Bennett fracture reduction? A: ≤ 1 mm = 83% asymptomatic at 7 yr; > 1 mm = 46% asymptomatic. Q: Why does the RCL not produce a Stener-equivalent lesion? A: The abductor pollicis aponeurosis lies more dorsal and doesn’t interpose between the torn RCL and bone.

title: Thumb Fractures + Ligament Injuries
heading: Ligament Injuries › CMC Dislocation
text: Rare; flexed + axially loaded MC; usually dorsal Closed reduce → percutaneous pin in thumb spica × 4 wk Persistent instability → Eaton FCR ligament reconstruction Chronic with OA → arthrodesis or arthroplasty

title: Thumb Fractures + Ligament Injuries
heading: Common Anatomy
text: Thumb CMC = unsupported by adjacent MCs → more unstable, but greater opposition/circumduction 2 phalanges → distal-to-proximal pinch line; force vector passes directly through CMC 80% of 1st MC fractures occur at base (poor proximal fixation) CMC stabilizers : volar (anterior) oblique ligament (“beak”), dorsoradial ligament

heading: Common Imaging

title: Thumb Fractures + Ligament Injuries

text: MCP collaterals : proper + accessory; proper attaches 3 mm distal to articular surface + 3 mm from volar cortex Distal UCL tear in 90% (vs more variable RCL tear site) Stener lesion : UCL fully torn + retracted + adductor pollicis aponeurosis interposed → blocks healing → SURGICAL RCL: no Stener-equivalent (abductor pollicis aponeurosis more dorsal, doesn’t interpose)

title: Thumb Fractures + Ligament Injuries
heading: Ligament Injuries › MCP Collateral Ligament Injuries
text: UCL 90%, RCL 10-42% Grading: I (pain, no laxity), II (laxity + firm endpoint), III (soft endpoint, complete) UCL (Skier’s Thumb) Valgus on abducted MCP Test : valgus stress at 0° (accessory) + 30° flexion (proper); > 35° laxity OR > 15° vs contralateral = unstable Gamekeeper’s thumb = chronic attritional UCL insufficiency Treatment - Grade I-II: thumb spica × 5-6 wk - Grade III (with Stener) → surgical (Stener prevents healing) - Grade III without Stener controversial — non-op in low-demand may be acceptable - Approach: S-incision; identify UCL + adductor aponeurosis + bony fragment - Repair: ligament advancement, transosseous tunnels/buttons, suture anchor (sliding for re-tensioning) — Krakow stitch - Internal brace (suture tape) augmentation: faster RTP for athletes (De Giacomo) - Werner 2-suture anchor in college football: skill players RTP 7 wk, linemen 4 wk - Chronic: tendon graft reconstruction or adductor pollicis advancement - Chronic with OA: arthrodesis RCL Forceful adduction Treatment principles same as UCL (no Stener equivalent) Reconstruction with APB advancement

title: Thumb Fractures + Ligament Injuries
heading: Fractures › Metacarpal
text: 25% of all MC fractures occur in the thumb; 80% at base Epibasal (Extra-articular Base) Apex dorsal (adductor pollicis + flexor pollicis brevis + APB) Reduce > 30° angulation (compensatory MCP hyperextension if untreated) Reduction: traction + extension + pronation + direct dorsal pressure Usually stable in thumb spica; CRPP if reduction not maintained Bennett Fracture (Intra-articular 2-Part) Volar ulnar fragment held by anterior oblique (beak) ligament → trapezium MC shaft + radial dorsal articular surface subluxates dorsally, proximally, radially (APL pull) Always unstable — even if reducible in cast Treatment - Anatomic reduction (≤ 1 mm step) → 83% asymptomatic at 7 yr ; > 1 mm → only 46% asymptomatic - Fluoroscopy underestimates true displacement (Capo cadaveric) - Closed reduction (traction + abduction + pronation + pressure on MC base) + CRPP usually sufficient - Pin configuration: K-wire perpendicular to MC long axis across CMC into trapezium (or 2nd MC base if ulnar fragment small); second K-wire from radial MC shaft across CMC into trapezium - ORIF if > 2 mm articular step persists (Wagner approach, screw if fragment allows) - Arthroscopic-assisted reduction (Culp) — direct articular visualization - Bennett fracture is inherently unstable; CRPP under fluoro after closed reduction is the standard - Goal is anatomic reduction (< 1 mm step) — sub-anatomic reductions have ~2× symptomatic rate at 7 years Rolando Fracture Y/T-pattern at base; volar-ulnar fragment + dorsa

title: Thumb Fractures + Ligament Injuries
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Robert’s view = essential for thumb base Bennett deforming forces: APL (proximal/radial/dorsal), adductor pollicis (adduction) Reduction maneuver: traction + abduction + pronation + dorsoradial MC base pressure Never accept any rotational deformity in thumb Stener lesion = absolute surgical indication; non-Stener grade III controversial Use 30° MCP flexion for UCL repair tensioning Bony Stener (fragment proximal to adductor aponeurosis) = surgical Acute Stener becomes scarred ≥ 3-4 wk — repair may still work if ligament minimally displaced For any acute thumb injury, get Robert’s view + stress views; Stener can sometimes be palpated; US is excellent confirmation

title: Thumb Fractures + Ligament Injuries
heading: Post-op / Rehab

title: Thumb Fractures + Ligament Injuries

heading: Acceptable Deformity (Phalanx)
text: Tolerance: sagittal > coronal > rotation Coronal angulation ≤ 15° Sagittal angulation ≤ 20° Shortening > 2-4 mm → swan neck or boutonniere risk No rotation tolerated

title: Phalangeal Fractures
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Phalangeal fractures are the most common hand fracture (incidence ~12.5/10,000); bimodal distribution — young males from sport/work injury and elderly from falls Phalanges = anchor points for flexor + extensor tendons → high adhesion + stiffness risk Distribution: middle phalanx least common Single nutrient vessel to middle third (proximal phalanx most consistent); disruption → nonunion or AVN of head Characteristic deformities: Proximal phalanx : apex volar (intrinsics flex proximal, extensor extends distal) Middle phalanx distal to FDS insertion : apex volar Middle phalanx proximal to FDS insertion : apex dorsal Distal phalanx : variable (FDP vs terminal extensor)

title: Phalangeal Fractures
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What’s the characteristic deformity of an extra-articular proximal phalanx shaft fracture? A: Apex volar — intrinsics flex proximal fragment, central slip + lateral bands extend distal fragment. Q: What angulation is acceptable in a phalangeal shaft fracture? A: Sagittal ≤ 20°, coronal ≤ 15°, shortening ≤ 2-4 mm. No rotation. Q: What does the Horton RCT tell us about long oblique/spiral proximal phalanx fractures? A: Closed reduction + percutaneous pinning gives equivalent outcomes to open + lag screw (motion, malunion). Q: What is the Seymour fracture and why is it considered open? A: Pediatric distal phalanx physeal fracture with nail bed laceration — the laceration through germinal matrix penetrates the joint; requires I&D + reduction + pinning. Q: Why is the intrinsic-plus position critical when splinting proximal phalanx fractures? A: MCP 70-90° flexion prevents collateral ligament contracture; PIP extension prevents PIP capsular contracture.

title: Phalangeal Fractures
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Stiffness most common complication Tendon adhesions (extensor + FDS/FDP) Malunion: correct at original site if < 3-4 wk; well-healed → MC-level osteotomy to avoid phalanx adhesions Nonunion rare in phalanges (infection, open, severe bone loss); tuft nonunion → HCS + bone graft Hardware failure, NV injury, infection Healing: clinical decrease in pain ~3-4 wk; radiographic 6-12 wk

title: Phalangeal Fractures
heading: Treatment › Distal Phalanx Shaft
text: Crush mechanism; usually transverse/oblique/comminuted Always check for nail bed injury — subungual hematoma evacuation for pain + bed inspection Displaced tuft → simple nail bed repair (6-0 chromic) + soft tissue closure Surgical skin glue equivalent to suture for nail bed (faster) DIP splint protection Seymour fracture (pediatric) : physeal fracture with nail bed laceration = open fracture → I&D + K-wire reduction

title: Phalangeal Fractures

text: Always check rotation (digits extended + flexed; compare contralateral) 1° metacarpal malrotation = 5° finger malrotation (Royle); phalangeal malrotation is similarly amplified by digit length and equally consequential clinically NV exam BEFORE digital block

title: Phalangeal Fractures
heading: Treatment › Fixation by Pattern
text: Transverse Multiple K-wires (crossed) OR intramedullary Avoid pinning across PIP/DIP unless necessary Oblique / Spiral (length ≥ 2× shaft width) Open + lag screw compression (multiple screws) Countersink heads; keep screws spaced apart (avoid iatrogenic fragmentation) Stable construct → gentle early motion at 2 wk Horton RCT : closed reduction + percutaneous pin = open + lag screw — equal outcomes (motion, malunion) Basar : screw-only > plate+screw for ROM + QuickDASH (longer immobilization but better motion) Very Proximal Proximal Phalanx Transmetacarpal head pinning : MCP flexed 70-90°, antegrade K-wires through MC head into proximal phalanx Faruqui: no significant difference vs extra-articular cross-pinning Comminuted / Periarticular Plate + screws or locked plate Dorsal approach: extensor split OR midaxial between lateral bands + central tendon Sacrifice lateral band if it improves exposure + reduces adhesions Expect plate removal + tenolysis later Plates only for severe injuries / soft tissue compromise (high adhesion rate) High-Energy Comminuted External fixation (temporary or definitive) Pin-track infection risk with prolonged use Bone graft (distal radius) after wound clean

title: Phalangeal Fractures
heading: Workup › Imaging

title: Phalangeal Fractures
heading: Treatment › Mallet (Distal Phalanx Articular Avulsion)
text: Soft tissue mallet : closed terminal extensor tendon injury → splint full DIP extension 6 wk full-time + 6 wk half-time Bony mallet : dorsal articular avulsion fragment off the distal phalanx Primary surgical indication: volar subluxation of the distal phalanx. Fragment > 50% articular surface is a secondary consideration; most bony mallets are managed non-operatively. Outcomes: non-op = good motion; op tends to lose more motion Barrera: Bony mallet — subluxation of the distal phalanx is the primary surgical indication. Fragment size (> 50% articular surface) is a secondary consideration that informs technique if you’re already operating but doesn’t by itself mandate surgery. Most bony mallets are non-operative — splint in extension 6 wk full + 6 wk half and they do well. Operating on a non-subluxated large fragment trades a stiff-but-aligned joint for a stiffer one. Intrinsic-plus splinting (MCP 70-90° flexed, PIPs extended) is essential for proximal phalanx fractures — MCP collateral contracture in extension is harder to correct than the fracture itself

title: Phalangeal Fractures
heading: Treatment › Non-displaced
text: Splint × ~3 wk + buddy tape + active motion Intrinsic-plus position : MCP 70-90° flexion + PIPs extended Wean to hand-based splint when stable Dynamic splinting acceptable in stable patterns (active flexion compresses; extensor tendon = dorsal tension band)

title: Phalangeal Fractures
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Check rotation at every visit Apex volar = proximal phalanx (intrinsics + extensor) — must reduce Lag screw works for long oblique with same outcomes as K-wire (Horton) Use plate only when nothing else works — adhesion + removal rates high Skin glue acceptable for nail bed repair (faster than suture) Don’t miss Seymour fracture in pediatric distal phalanx — physeal + nail bed = open Hand therapy referral within first week — edema control + protected motion within the construct’s constraints prevent the stiffness that defines this injury

title: Phalangeal Fractures
heading: Post-op / Rehab

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Bicondylar hinge ; ROM 0-120° 85% of grasp motion comes from PIP Primary stabilizers : tongue-in-groove articular geometry + proper collateral ligaments Secondary : volar plate, accessory collaterals, surrounding soft tissue

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Board-Style Questions
text: Q: What % of grasp motion comes from the PIP joint? A: 85%. Q: Describe the Elson test and how to interpret it. A: PIP held 90° flexed; patient extends against resistance; examiner tests DIP for resistance. Rigid DIP extension = positive = central slip rupture. Q: At what % of articular involvement does a dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation become unstable and require surgery? A: > 50% volar lip articular involvement is unstable; 30-50% is tenuous; < 30% usually stable. Q: What is the donor site for the hemi-hamate osteochondral autograft? A: Dorsal distal hamate — its concavity matches the volar lip cup of the middle phalanx base. Q: What is the major contraindication to volar plate arthroplasty (Eaton-Malerich)? A: Articular surface involvement > 50% (joint becomes unstable without bony buttress).

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Classification of Injuries
text: Strain/sprain (collateral or volar plate) Dislocations (dorsal, lateral, volar) — no fracture Fracture-dislocations Pilon fracture = V + dorsal margin fractures of middle phalanx base; splay in both planes

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Stiffness most common (every option) Permanent PIP girth increase Flexion contracture Swan neck (volar plate detachment → loss of checkrein) Posttraumatic arthritis Tenolysis often needed Salvage: arthrodesis, silicone arthroplasty, resurfacing arthroplasty

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Pure Dislocations › Dorsal Dislocation (most common)
text: Reduce with traction + volar pressure Generally stable after reduction without fracture Simple + stable: buddy tape or 10° extension-block × 3-4 wk Unstable in extension → dorsal blocking splint + immediate active flexion

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Dorsal Fracture-Dislocations of PIP (Volar Lip Fracture of Middle Phalanx)
text: Decision based on % articular involvement + flexion needed for stability: Articular % Stability Treatment < 30% Usually stable Dorsal block splint, extend 10°/wk 30-50% Tenuous Dorsal block splint OR surgery > 50% Unstable Surgery > 30° flexion needed for congruence Unstable Surgery

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Workup › Elson Test (central slip)
text: PIP held flexed 90° → patient extends against resistance → examiner tests DIP for resistance to flexion Positive = rigid DIP extension (intact central slip = lateral bands relax = DIP floppy; ruptured = lateral bands tighten = DIP stiff)

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Inspect alignment; skin puckering = soft tissue entrapment = irreducible Tendon integrity (resting tension + tenodesis) Full extension test critical for volar dislocations (boutonniere risk) Dorsal dislocation: usually unstable in extension; palmar dislocation: unstable in flexion Document degree of flexion needed for congruent joint

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: True lateral PIP critical Dorsal V sign = subtle dorsal subluxation True AP for coronal

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Pure Dislocations › Lateral Dislocation
text: Reducible → buddy tape + early protected ROM Irreducible → volar rotatory category

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Document degree of flexion needed for joint congruence — drives treatment Volar dislocation = check central slip → splint extension 3 wk before declaring safe Dorsal V sign on lateral = subtle dorsal subluxation 50% volar lip articular involvement → hemi-hamate autograft is one of the standard options (along with DEF, ORIF, VPA depending on fragment quality) Dorsal block splint extends 10°/wk to full extension at 6-8 wk Pilon = stability first, congruity second Adjacent joint motion immediately to avoid DIP stiffness Never tell a patient they’ll have full motion back

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Pilon Fractures
text: Complete dissociation of articular surface from middle phalanx base Dorsal-palmar + radio-ulnar splay → inherently unstable Primary goal: joint stability + alignment (anatomic articular congruity is secondary) Options: ORIF, DEF, combinations Locking + condylar plates successful Aggressive ORIF risks may outweigh DEF benefits PIP motion 80-90° outcomes

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Early motion within 1 wk prevents adhesions Adjacent joint motion immediately (DIP stiffness often underreported) Stable construct → active-assisted exercises at 3-6 wk Flexion contracture stretching + nighttime extension splinting at 4-6 wk Elastic garments for edema; desensitization Counsel all patients pre-op about permanent PIP girth increase, some loss of motion, and arthritis risk regardless of treatment

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Dorsal Fracture-Dislocations of PIP (Volar Lip Fracture of Middle Phalanx) › Surgical Options (no clear superiority)
text: Dorsal block pinning (Waris 41 pts at 5 yr: PIP arc 80°, 6° contracture, 29% recurrent subluxation, 10% severe arthritis) Dynamic external fixation (“pins + rubber”): ligamentotaxis, immediate motion; 15-25% pin track infection, 25% early arthritis ORIF : large fragments, small screws, rigid early ROM; PIP arc 70-85%; failure up to 9% Volar Plate Arthroplasty (Eaton-Malerich) : excise volar lip, advance volar plate; contraindicated > 50% articular (instability risk); PIP arc 70-90° Hemi-Hamate Osteochondral Autograft (Williams-Hastings) : dorsal distal hamate matches volar lip cup; for > 50% volar lip defect, comminution, or salvage; PIP arc 65-85°

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Pure Dislocations › Volar Dislocation (rare, unstable)
text: Boutonniere risk from central slip injury Often involves central slip + volar plate + ≥ 1 collateral Splint PIP in full extension × 3 wk with serial lateral XR for re-dislocation Re-dislocation → pin PIP in extension × 3-4 more wk Total ~6-8 wk splinting

title: PIP Joint Dislocations and Fracture-Dislocations
heading: Pure Dislocations › Volar Rotatory Dislocation
text: Proximal phalanx rotates around intact collateral Often irreducible (condyle trapped between central slip + lateral band OR collateral button-holes) Operative if irreducible Any volar dislocation: check central slip integrity (Elson test if possible at presentation; MRI/US if unclear); splint full extension for 3 wk before declaring boutonniere risk averted

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Proximal row (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform): no tendon attachments — intercalated segment; position dictated by geometry + ligaments Distal row (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate): rigid platform with negligible intercarpal motion Gilula’s lines : smooth concentric arcs along proximal/distal row joint surfaces on PA; disruption = instability Extrinsic ligaments : volar (RSC, LRL, SRL, ulnocarpal complex) > dorsal (DRC, DIC) in structural strength; dorsal ligaments more proprioceptive Space of Poirier : capsular weakness between RSC and LRL — lunate dislocates volarly through here SLIL : dorsal strongest; LTIL : volar strongest Dart-thrower’s motion (DTM) : natural wrist axis (radial extension → ulnar flexion); minimal proximal row motion through this arc

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: In Mayfield’s progressive perilunar instability, what structure fails in stage III? — A: The lunotriquetral interosseous ligament. Q: A patient with midcarpal instability demonstrates a painful clunk as the wrist moves into ulnar deviation with the proximal row snapping from flexion into extension. What is this sign called? — A: The catch-up clunk (palmar midcarpal instability). Q: What is the reported nonunion rate for lunotriquetral arthrodesis? — A: 41% (Shin series). Q: A perilunate fracture-dislocation with a scaphoid waist fracture is classified as what type of arc injury? — A: Greater arc injury. Q: What surgical option for palmar midcarpal instability best preserves dart-thrower’s motion? — A: Radiolunate fusion.

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Carpal Instability Adaptive (CIA)
text: Most commonly from distal radius malunion (dorsal tilt → DISI → midcarpal catch-up clunk) Treatment: corrective osteotomy of distal radius; 3D virtual planning available

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Carpal Instability Complex (Perilunate Injuries)
text: Mayfield stages (radial → ulnar) : I = SL disruption; II = capitate dislocation (space of Poirier opens); III = LT dissociation; IV = lunate dislocation Lesser arc = purely ligamentous; greater arc = fractures through surrounding bones (most commonly transscaphoid) PLIND (perilunate injuries non-dislocated): no capitate-lunate dislocation on lateral; midcarpal osteochondral loose bodies are a clue Up to 25% historically missed; lateral radiograph most diagnostic (“spilled teacup” sign) ORIF : combined volar + dorsal approach. Volar first (CTR + volar capsule [space of Poirier] repair), then dorsal (joystick K-wires to reduce the SL, then 0.062” K-wires for definitive stabilization). Arthroscopic-assisted fixation feasible for PLIND and select PLD (Herzberg stages 1-2A) Post-op: cast 2 months → wrist brace + gentle motion; buried K-wire removal at 3 months Despite severity, 10-15 yr outcomes often satisfactory; delay in treatment = worst prognostic factor Barrera: Perilunate repair construct — combined volar + dorsal approach. Start volar: CTR (median nerve is almost always under pressure), then repair the volar capsule (space of Poirier). Go dorsal: joystick K-wires into scaphoid + lunate to reduce the SL under direct vision, then 0.062” pins for definitive stabilization. Cast 2 months, transition to wrist brace + gentle motion, buried K-wire removal at 3 months.

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Classification
text: Larsen (1995) — 6 parameters: chronicity, constancy, etiology, location, direction, pattern CID (carpal instability dissociative): within a row (SL, LT) CIND (carpal instability nondissociative): between rows (midcarpal, radiocarpal) CIC (carpal instability complex): perilunate injuries spanning both CIA (carpal instability adaptive): secondary to extracarpal pathology (distal radius malunion)

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Carpal Instability Nondissociative (CIND) › Combined Midcarpal Instability (CMCI)
text: Young women with laxity; VISI deformity + dorsal subluxation on provocative testing May respond to volar ligamentous reefing (Apergis: 13/14 excellent); but at 5-8 yr follow-up, no difference surgical vs nonsurgical

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Carpal Instability Nondissociative (CIND) › Dorsal Midcarpal Instability (DMCI / CLIP Wrist)
text: Dorsal capitate subluxation on lunate (CIND-DISI) Pain with heavy lifting + power grasp in supination Johnson-Carroll: space of Poirier obliteration (6 excellent/11 outcomes) Treatment: primarily nonsurgical

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Lunotriquetral Interosseous Ligament Injury
text: Less common than SL; often associated with TFCC tears and ulnar impaction Geissler classification applies (same as SL) VISI pattern (lunate flexion) — only with complete LTIL + secondary stabilizer failure Cadaveric: 30% LTIL perforation in patients > 60 yo Exam : LT ballottement (Reagan test), LT shear (Kleinman test), LT compression; ulnar-sided wrist pain Imaging : disrupted Gilula’s arcs I/II, proximal triquetral migration; diastasis rare even with instability Treatment ladder : Conservative: immobilization (pisiform-supported cast), therapy, CSI Arthroscopic debridement + pinning (80% success, Osterman series) Ligament reconstruction (distally based ECU strip through bone tunnels) — 69% 5-yr survival (Shin) LT arthrodesis: 41% nonunion rate — generally avoided Ulnar shortening osteotomy: effective when ulnocarpal abutment coexists (83% good-to-excellent, Mirza) Barrera: For suspected TFCC injuries with associated LT symptoms, start with the standard ladder: 4 weeks brace → Wrist Widget + OT → MRI without contrast → CSI → surgery as last resort. Most stable-DRUJ injuries respond to immobilization and bracing. The LT component often improves in parallel with TFCC-directed conservative treatment.

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Carpal Instability Nondissociative (CIND) › Palmar Midcarpal Instability (PMCI)
text: Most common CIND; often in generalized ligamentous laxity “Catch-up clunk” : proximal row lags in flexion during ulnar deviation → snaps into extension “Kettle sign”: difficulty holding heavy objects in ulnar deviation Radiographs often normal; dynamic fluoroscopy demonstrates clunk Treatment : primarily nonsurgical (6+ months); ECU/FCU strengthening, pisiform-padded orthosis Surgical: dorsal capsular plication (von Schroeder: durable improvement at 35 months); radiolunate fusion preserves DTM; soft tissue reconstruction has high failure rate (6/9 in Lichtman series)

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Always get a true lateral radiograph — most perilunate injuries are diagnosed here PLIND lesions: look for midcarpal osteochondral loose bodies as a diagnostic clue LT arthrodesis has unacceptably high nonunion (41%) — reconstruction or ulnar shortening preferred Midcarpal instability is primarily nonsurgical — commit to 6 months of therapy before considering surgery For radiocarpal fracture-dislocations, protect the volar ligament repair for 3 full months Dart-thrower’s motion rehab is relevant across multiple instability patterns

title: Wrist Dissociation and Instability (non-SL)
heading: Radiocarpal Instability / Fracture-Dislocations
text: High-energy; dorsal dislocation more common Dumontier classification : type 1 (< 1/3 scaphoid facet, RSC avulsion) vs type 2 (> 1/3 facet fragment) Type 1: volar ligament repair + dorsal spanning plate protection (3 months before plate removal) Type 2: ORIF of radial styloid fragment restores stability
