title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: DRUJ : diarthrodial trochoid joint; intrinsically unstable; ulnar head (convex, 10 mm curvature) articulates with sigmoid notch of radius (concave, 15 mm curvature) Sigmoid notch morphology (axial plane): flat face (42%), C-type (30%), S-type (14%), ski slope (12%) Tolat coronal types : type I parallel (55%), type II oblique (33%), type III reverse oblique (12%) Ulnar fovea : center of forearm rotation axis; attachment site for deep RUL fibers (ligamentum subcruentum) TFCC components : central articular disc, dorsal + volar RULs, meniscus homologue, ulnar collateral ligament, ulnocarpal ligaments, ECU subsheath floor RULs = primary DRUJ stabilizers; each has superficial (styloid) and deep (foveal) components; both must be injured for severe unidirectional instability Forearm rotation : anatomic arc 150-170° (full passive max pronation → max supination); functional arc 140-150° (Morrey, Sennwald) — the range used for ADLs and the target for reconstruction < 10% ulnar head contact at extremes of rotation; max contact (60%) at neutral Force transmission : radius carries majority; ulna 3-34% depending on ulnar variance Barrera: When teaching forearm rotation, distinguish the anatomic arc (150-170°) from the functional arc (140-150°) . Textbooks conflate the two. The functional arc is what predicts disability and what you’re trying to restore in DRUJ reconstruction or distal radius malunion correction. A patient who loses 30° from anatomic max still keeps a working arc.

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Associated Injury Patterns
text: Galeazzi fracture : DRUJ instability in 55% if fracture < 7.5 cm from articular surface; stabilize radius first, then assess DRUJ Essex-Lopresti : radial head fracture + IOM rupture + DRUJ disruption; ulnar-positive variance is a clue; radial head replacement + DRUJ repair ± IOM reconstruction Distal radius malunion : most common cause of chronic DRUJ dysfunction; dorsal angulation > 20-30° and radial shortening > 3-5 mm → DRUJ instability

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: Which Palmer class TFCC tear causes DRUJ instability and involves avulsion from the ulnar attachment? — A: Class IB (ulnar avulsion/peripheral tear). Q: A Galeazzi fracture is defined as a fracture of the distal third of the radius with what associated injury? — A: Dislocation of the DRUJ (dorsal or volar). Q: What position of immobilization provides maximal DRUJ stability after reduction of a dorsal DRUJ dislocation? — A: Supination. Q: What is the gold standard imaging study for evaluating DRUJ instability? — A: CT with bilateral comparison in neutral, supination, and pronation. Q: In an Essex-Lopresti injury, what three structures are disrupted? — A: Radial head, interosseous membrane, and DRUJ (TFCC).

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Classification
text: Palmer classification of TFCC tears : Class I (traumatic) : IA = central perforation (no DRUJ instability); IB = ulnar avulsion (can destabilize DRUJ); IC = distal avulsion (ulnocarpal ligaments); ID = radial avulsion Class II (degenerative) : IIA = wear; IIB = wear + chondromalacia; IIC = perforation + chondromalacia; IID = + LT perforation; IIE = + ulnocarpal arthritis

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Ballottement/shuck test : stabilize radius, translate ulna dorsal-palmar in neutral, pronation, supination; compare contralateral Piano key sign : pronated forearm, press ulna volarly → springs back like piano key DRUJ compression test : compress ulna against sigmoid notch + rotate forearm → pain/crepitus Fovea sign : press soft spot between FCU, ECU, triquetrum, ulnar head → pain = TFCC pathology Table-top test : push up from seated → dorsal dimple sign = instability

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Workup › History
text: Dorsal/volar dislocation mechanism: hyperpronation → dorsal; hypersupination → volar Associated injuries: distal radius fracture (most common), Galeazzi fracture, Essex-Lopresti injury Ulnar styloid fractures accompany 60% of distal radius fractures; base fractures with > 2 mm displacement or foveal involvement may destabilize DRUJ

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: True lateral : pisoscaphocapitate relationship; ulna normally 2 mm dorsal to radius; > 6 mm = instability CT (gold standard) : bilateral comparison in neutral/supination/pronation MRI/MR arthrography : foveal attachment assessment; sensitivity debated Arthroscopy : trampoline test (central disc tension), hook test (foveal competence), suction test

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Acute isolated DRUJ dislocation: closed reduction + above-elbow immobilization 4-6 weeks in position of stability (dorsal dislocation → supination; volar → pronation) Subacute/chronic: wrist brace, FCU/ECU strengthening Barrera: For TFCC injuries with a stable DRUJ, use the standard treatment ladder: 4 weeks rigid brace → Wrist Widget + OT → MRI without contrast if still symptomatic → CSI (Kenalog 10 mg/mL + 1% lido, never Depo) → surgery only as last resort with positive MRI and refractory symptoms.

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: TFCC Repair - Peripheral repair: outside-in arthroscopic technique; debride synovitis, PDS sutures through capsule + disc - Foveal repair (deep): arthroscopic bone tunnel repair (preferred) or open anchor into fovea - Open foveal repair (Barrera technique): hockey stick incision → double opposing inverted L capsulotomies with transverse limbs at the joint interface to protect the TFCC → big bite of TFCC with 2-0 PDS → two bone tunnels with 1.6 mm K-wire from fovea out the ulnar neck → pass suture through tunnels → tie down with forearm in neutral rotation → dorsal capsulorrhaphy / tightening for added stability Barrera: Open foveal repair construct: hockey-stick incision, double opposing inverted L capsulotomies (transverse limbs at the joint interface to protect the TFCC), big bite of TFCC with 2-0 PDS , two bone tunnels with a 1.6 mm K-wire from the fovea out the ulnar neck , tie down with forearm in neutral , then dorsal capsulorrhaphy for added DRUJ stability. The inverted-L design is the part residents miss — draw it on the skin before incision. - Comparable outcomes open vs arthroscopic DRUJ Ligament Reconstruction (Adams procedure) - Indication: chronic instability with irreparable TFCC - Palmaris longus tendon graft through bone tunnels in radius (dorsal-to-volar) and ulna (fovea-to-lateral neck) - Graft passed around ulnar neck in opposite directions, tensioned in neutral rotation, tied - Post-op: long-arm orthosis → cast; short-arm at 4 wk; activities at 4 mo; heavy

title: DRUJ Injury and Reconstruction
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Both dorsal and volar RULs must be injured for complete unidirectional instability After distal radius ORIF, always check DRUJ stability intraoperatively Ulnar styloid tip fractures are generally benign; base fractures may destabilize the DRUJ The hook test is the most sensitive/specific arthroscopic test for foveal detachment (Atzei) CT is superior to lateral radiographs for diagnosing DRUJ subluxation (10° rotation can falsely normalize lateral) When reconstructing the DRUJ, address any sigmoid notch deficiency or distal radius malunion first

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Layers (inside out): endoneurium (surrounds axon + Schwann cell basement membrane) → perineurium (blood-brain barrier extension; fascicles “pooch” when cut) → inner epineurium (cushion) → outer epineurium (vessels on surface = alignment landmarks) Fascicular topography: Sunderland described intraneural plexus with branching/interconnections; more recent work shows functional segregation even proximally — critical for nerve transfer design Blood supply: epineurial vessels → extensive internal network; nerve tolerates long-distance mobilization without ischemia (redundant supply reconstitutes in days) Wallerian degeneration : initiates 24-48 hrs post-injury; Schwann cells transdifferentiate, form Bands of Bungner (guidance channels); mediators include IL-4, IL-10, NGF, CNTF, GDNF Motor axons show slight preference for motor endoneurial tubes (limited specificity) 1% of functional potential lost per week of denervation ; after ~18 months, muscle irreversibly replaced by fibro-adipose tissue Regeneration rate: 1 mm/day (1 inch/month, 1.5 ft/year) Proximal injuries = worse prognosis (longer regeneration distance, axon “steal” by proximal muscles)

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Board-Style Questions (3-5)
text: Q: A patient sustains a closed humeral shaft fracture with complete radial nerve palsy. NCS/EMG at 3 weeks shows absent conduction distal to injury with no fibrillations. What does this suggest? — A: Too early to differentiate neurapraxia from axonotmesis; distal conduction may persist 3-11 days post-transection, and fibrillations take several weeks to develop. Repeat at 6 weeks. Q: What is the maximum gap length for which a synthetic conduit is generally reliable for digital nerve reconstruction? — A: < 2.5 cm (results decline significantly beyond 8-12 mm in some series). Q: A 30-year-old sustains a sharp laceration of the ulnar nerve at the wrist. Primary repair is performed. At what rate should you expect axon regeneration, and when might intrinsic function return? — A: 1 mm/day; ~8-10 months to hand intrinsics, though proximal ulnar injuries have a dismal intrinsic recovery prognosis regardless. Q: Intraoperative nerve conduction testing across a neuroma-in-continuity demonstrates an action potential. What is the recommended management? — A: Continued observation; presence of an action potential across the lesion is associated with a 90% chance of continued spontaneous recovery. Q: After 18 months of muscle denervation, why is nerve repair unlikely to restore meaningful motor function? — A: Schwann cell senescence, loss of endoneurial guidance channels, dispersion of ACh receptor clusters, satellite cell exhaustion, and irreversible fibro-adipose replacement of muscle.

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Classification
text: Sunderland (modified by MacKinnon) : I (neurapraxia) : myelin/local environment only; recovers minutes-months II (axonotmesis) : axons disrupted, endoneurial tubes intact; spontaneous recovery III : endoneurial tubes disrupted; variable recovery IV : perineurium disrupted; no spontaneous recovery V (neurotmesis) : complete rupture; requires surgery VI (MacKinnon) : mixed pattern across zone of injury — hardest to manage

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Digital nerve primary repair : mean static 2PD ~10.6 mm (normal contralateral 4.4 mm); 48-72% good/excellent; sharp > crush; age matters; children approach 100% normal sensation Digital nerve gaps ≤ 3 cm : autograft 70-100% S3+/S4; ANA 83-84% S3+/S4; conduits 50-89% Mixed/motor nerves : primary repair 72% ≥ grade 3 (ulnar), 85% (median/radial); early repair > delayed Autograft for mixed nerves : useful motor (M3+) in 63-81%; gaps > 4.5 cm (ulnar), 5 cm (median), 8 cm (radial) = worse ANA for mixed : 77-81% meaningful recovery (M3+); only 40-50% achieve M4+ Sural nerve harvest: persistent sensory loss in 93%; allodynia in 50% (few consider it a major problem) Neuroma management: reconstruction preferred when distal stump available; TMR (targeted muscle reinnervation) gaining enthusiasm; centro-central repair for digital stump neuromas

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: Wait 2-3 weeks post-injury for meaningful NCS/EMG (Wallerian degeneration must progress) Neurapraxia: intact conduction distal to injury, no fibrillations Axonotmesis/neurotmesis: loss of distal conduction, fibrillations on EMG Cannot reliably distinguish Sunderland II from III/IV early 3-4 months : intraoperative nerve-to-nerve conduction across zone of injury; action potential present = 90% chance of continued recovery

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Serial exams (monthly): active ROM, isolated muscle strength, sensory testing, Tinel tracking Progressing Tinel = controversial but useful if documented with focal locations + measurements Neuroma pain (mechanical, triggered by direct stimulus/stretch) vs neuropathic pain (burning, tingling, nocturnal, cortical imprinting) — local block differentiates

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Treatment › Gap Bridging
text: Conduits : for digital/sensory nerves, gaps < 2.5 cm; collagen, PGA, polycaprolactone; fibrin clot scaffold unreliable > 15 mm Acellular nerve allograft (ANA) : 3D neural architecture advantage; digital/sensory up to 5-7 cm; growing use in mixed nerves; 84% S3+/S4 for short sensory gaps; autograft still gold standard for gaps > 7 cm Autograft : sural nerve = workhorse (30-40 cm per leg); cable graft technique for larger nerves; harvest 15-20% longer than defect; vascularized grafts theoretically better but not widely adopted Nerve transfers : sacrifice redundant nerve for critical function; especially useful for proximal injuries, long gaps, hostile tissue beds

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: US or MR neurography to identify complete ruptures (surgical indication) MRI advances may distinguish injury grades but clinical utility unproven

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Sunderland I-II with NCS/EMG confirmation or early clinical recovery: observation Passive ROM to prevent joint stiffness; strengthening once any recovery detected Gabapentin, pregabalin, amitriptyline for neuropathic pain (minimize narcotics) Mirror therapy + desensitization for neuroma/neuropathic pain

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Treatment › Operative
text: Indications : laceration with deficit, confirmed neurotmesis, closed injuries without recovery at 3-4 months Repair ASAP to minimize axotomy/denervation effects + stump retraction Avulsion/blast/GSW: wait 2-3 weeks for zone demarcation; acute repair of avulsed radial nerves = universal failure Tension > 8-15% = decreased perfusion, impaired Schwann cell function, stunted regeneration Coaptation tools : Suture (epineurial > fascicular in most situations) Fibrin glue (fast, equivalent in animal studies; risk of catastrophic failure; not FDA-approved for nerve) Connectors (entubulation improves alignment, protects repair site, may auto-correct malalignment)

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Neurapraxia vs axonotmesis cannot be distinguished in first 2-3 weeks — early EDX has minimal value Fascicles “pooch” from cut nerves due to perineurial pressure — inspect for this to confirm healthy fascicular pattern during resection Epineurial vessels = key alignment landmarks during repair Conduit gap > 15 mm for digital nerves = less predictable fibrin clot scaffold Radial nerve has best prognosis; ulnar nerve (especially proximal) has worst ANA vs autograft: unsettled debate; patient preference (cadaver tissue vs donor site morbidity) often decides

title: Nerve Injury and Repair
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Protective immobilization 3 weeks post-coaptation (60% burst strength at 8 wk in rodents, 77% at 4 wk in primates) Early motion OK after digital nerve repair (does not affect outcomes) Protected early ROM takes precedence if concurrent flexor tendon repair Emphasis on maintaining supple joints, pain control, nerve-modulating medications

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: High median palsy (proximal to AIN): loss of FCR, FDS, FDP index (±long), FPL, PQ, thenar muscles, lumbricals 1-2 → index finger rests in full extension, thumb loses opposition + IP flexion Low median palsy (distal to AIN): thenar muscles + lumbricals 1-2 only → normal digital cascade, thenar wasting, lost opposition; clawing rare (interossei compensate) Wrist-level injury : primarily sensory (thumb through radial ring); palmar cutaneous branch spared; thenar wasting Long finger FDP often has dual ulnar + median innervation → may retain flexion Deep head FPB often dual innervated → some palmar abduction preserved even in median palsy

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A patient with high median nerve palsy has index and long fingers resting in extension while ring and small fingers maintain normal cascade. What muscles are denervated? — A: FDP to index (AIN), FDS to all digits (median), FPL (AIN), pronator teres, FCR, PQ, thenar muscles, lumbricals 1-2. Ring/small FDP are ulnar-innervated and preserved. Q: Which opponensplasty is preferred for a patient with combined median and ulnar nerve palsy? — A: EIP (Burkhalter) — it is radial nerve-innervated and does not require a pulley, making it reliable when both median and ulnar motors are unavailable. Q: What is the preferred nerve transfer to restore forearm pronation in an isolated pronator teres palsy? — A: ECRB branch to PT nerve — synergistic function (wrist extension + pronation occur together) facilitates intuitive motor re-education. Q: After a high median nerve injury, the long finger retains DIP flexion. Why? — A: Long finger FDP often has dual innervation from both the AIN (median) and ulnar nerve; the ulnar contribution preserves active DIP flexion.

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Nerve transfer outcomes: ECRB→AIN achieves M3-M4 finger/thumb flexion at 12-24 months; brachialis→AIN similar EIP opponensplasty: reliable but EDC subluxation if extensor hood not repaired; EIP absent in 4% FDS opponensplasty: adequate length and excursion; risk of swan neck and friction at pulley site Sural nerve harvest: persistent sensory loss in most (93%); allodynia in 50% but rarely clinically significant Sensory nerve transfer: risk of abnormal sensation, painful donor site, poor cortical reorientation FDP side-car: cannot achieve independent index flexion; transection prevents recovery if nerve regenerates

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: Wait ≥ 3 weeks post-injury; NCS/EMG distinguishes neurapraxia from axonotmetic injury Cannot reliably differentiate Sunderland II from III/IV early Intraoperative NAP across neuroma-in-continuity: positive = 90% continued recovery

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Sensory: thumb, index, long, radial ring (volar + dorsal tips); palmar cutaneous branch → thenar eminence + radial palm (high vs low localization) Motor: test opposition (APB), FPL (thumb IP flexion), FDP index (DIP flexion), pronation Resting cascade : high palsy = index (±long) in full extension; low palsy = normal cascade + thenar wasting

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Repair
text: Same principles as NV-01: resect to healthy fascicles, tension-free, fascicular alignment, epineurial suture Avulsion/blast: wait 2-3 weeks for demarcation; cable graft for gaps Sural nerve = workhorse donor; 30-40 cm per leg; cable graft technique for larger nerves

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Transfers for Motor
text: ECRB branch → AIN : restores extrinsic finger/thumb flexion (FDP index, FPL, PQ) Brachialis branch (musculocutaneous) → AIN or PT : for high injuries ECRB → PT nerve : restores pronation (simultaneous wrist extension + pronation = intuitive re-education) ADM ulnar motor branch → recurrent median motor branch : restores opposition (El-Haj) Nerve transfer technique pearl : check with anesthesia pre-op about avoiding long-acting paralytics — intraoperative stimulation required. At 0.5 mA the donor should fire strongly; at 2.0 mA the recipient target should have zero response. “Donor distal, recipient proximal” for tension-free coaptation.

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Transfers for Sensation
text: Critical: restore sensation to radial index + ulnar thumb for precision pinch Ulnar 4th web space → median 1st web space (end-to-end, with reverse end-to-side for donor recovery) Dorsal cutaneous ulnar → median 1st/2nd web space fascicles (forearm level) Radial sensory branches → ulnar digital thumb + radial digital index (dorsal-to-palmar transfer) FDMA flap (innervated by dorsoradial sensory nerve) for thumb pulp resurfacing — sensate but donor morbidity limits use

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Neurapraxic/axonotmetic with evidence of recovery: observation + passive ROM Opponens splint (thumb in palmar abduction, slight pronation, slight MP flexion) Buddy straps for index/long finger flexion deficit Consider non-operative if minimal functional deficit or patient has adapted well (e.g., strong pulp-to-side pinch in quadriplegia)

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Index finger in full extension at rest = pathognomonic for high median palsy Thenar wasting + normal digital cascade = low median palsy EIP opponensplasty = best choice for combined median-ulnar injuries (radial nerve innervated) Camitz = abduction only, not true opposition — quick addition during open CTR in severe CTS with thenar atrophy Don’t forget to test deep head FPB (often ulnar innervated) — some palmar abduction may be preserved Full passive ROM at all joints required before any tendon transfer

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: All opponensplasties: thumb spica 4-6 weeks (thumb palmarly abducted, flexed, pronated, wrist neutral); therapy at 4-6 wk; strengthening at 8 wk FDP side-car: dorsal blocking splint (digits slightly flexed, wrist neutral) x 4-6 weeks Nerve transfers: motor re-education starts at 3 weeks (donor activation, mirror therapy, bilateral exercises)

title: Median Nerve Injury, Repair, and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Tendon Transfers — Opposition
text: EIP Opponensplasty (Burkhalter) — preferred for trauma/combined median-ulnar palsy - EIP harvested at index MCP (ulnar side of sagittal band); rerouted dorsal-ulnar → palmar-radial around ulna; Pulvertaft weave into APB insertion - No pulley needed (ulna redirects); radial-nerve innervated (independent of median/ulnar) - Drawbacks: dorsal ulnar sensory nerve at risk; crosses over carpal tunnel scar FDS Ring Opponensplasty — low median palsy only - FDS harvested through palmar incision; redirected through FCU pulley or Guyon canal/palmar fascia; subcutaneous tunnel across palm → APB insertion - Excellent excursion; all palmar incisions - Drawbacks: swan neck risk (hypermobile patients); median-innervated donor (unavailable in high palsy or combined injury) ADQ (Huber) Opponensplasty — also for congenital thumb hypoplasia - Ulnar-innervated; restores thenar esthetic; unique cosmetic advantage - Line of pull favors flexion/pronation > abduction - Drawbacks: limited excursion; pedicle at risk; compresses Guyon canal Camitz (PL → APB) — quick, done with open CTR - Primarily provides abduction only (not true opposition) - PL absent in up to 20%; cannot use in high median palsy

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Most common peripheral nerve injury with long-bone fractures — 11.8% of humeral shaft fractures Injury at junction of middle/distal thirds of humerus (least mobile segment) Holstein-Lewis (distal humeral shaft) fractures: up to 25% radial nerve palsy 71% of humeral shaft fracture radial palsies resolve with observation Reinnervation order (proximal→distal): BR → ECRL → ECRB → EDC → ECU → EDQ → APL → EPL → EPB → EIP Radial nerve has best recovery prognosis of the three major UE nerves: shorter distance to motor end plates, larger caliber, distinct fascicular organization, motor-predominant with similar target muscles

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A patient sustains a closed mid-shaft humerus fracture with complete wrist drop. At 6 weeks, EMG shows no MUPs in radial-innervated muscles. What is the management? — A: Continue observation to 3 months total; 71% of closed fracture radial palsies recover spontaneously. Splint with cock-up orthosis + maintain passive ROM. Q: In a FCR-based tendon transfer for radial nerve palsy, which tendon powers wrist extension, finger extension, and thumb extension? — A: PT → ECRB (wrist), FCR → EDC (fingers), PL → EPL (thumb). Q: What is the primary advantage of nerve transfer over tendon transfer for radial nerve palsy? — A: Nerve transfer restores independent finger extension, avoids sacrifice of wrist flexion strength, and avoids the radial deviation deformity seen with FCU-based tendon transfers. Q: What radial nerve graft gap length is associated with significantly worse outcomes? — A: > 8 cm (Petkovic); for median nerve > 5 cm, for ulnar nerve > 4.5 cm.

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Tendon transfer: reliable, time-proven; potential bowstringing (especially PL→EPL), radial deviation (FCU method), stiffness Nerve transfer: less dissection, no strength loss, independent finger extension; but 9-12 month wait Jain 2023 systematic review : TT clinical success 82% vs nerve transfer 59% vs nerve grafts Bertelli 2020 : nerve transfers better — TT group had wrist flexion limitation (9/13), permanent radial deviation (5/13), 50% needed wrist flexion for full finger extension

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: Begin 6 weeks post-injury; MUPs on EMG = potential for recovery No MUPs at 3 months → explore

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Workup › Exam
text: High radial palsy : loss of BR, ECRL, ECRB, EDC, ECU, EIP, thumb extensors → no wrist/finger/thumb MCP extension + decreased 2PD dorsal hand Very proximal: also loses triceps + posterior arm sensation PIN palsy : BR + ECRL preserved → wrist extends with radial deviation; SBRN intact MRC grading; donor must be ≥ M4 (loses one grade with transfer)

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Repair/Reconstruction
text: Primary end-to-end : ideal; 91% ≥ M3 with primary suture (Murovic) Tension-free; resect to healthy fascicles; humeral shortening for 1-2 cm gaps Avulsions = universally failed with acute repair (inadequate debridement) Autograft : sural nerve or medial antebrachial cutaneous; Berger: 77% M4-M5 with interfascicular graft (avg 6.6 cm) Gaps > 8 cm = significantly worse outcomes (Petkovic) Open injuries, concomitant vascular injury, no recovery at 3 months → surgical exploration

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Transfers (Median-to-Radial)
text: FDS branch → ECRB (wrist extension) FCR branch → PIN (finger + thumb extension) “Donor distal, recipient proximal” — curvilinear proximal forearm incision Ray & Mackinnon (19 pts) : 18/19 M4+ wrist extension at 20 mo; 12/19 M4+ finger/thumb extension Ideal window: 3-6 months from injury; reinnervation goal within 12-18 months Advantages: faster proximal-level recovery, avoids injured field, no graft, independent finger extension 9 patients also received concurrent PT→ECRB tendon transfer as dynamic internal splint Key teaching point : nerve transfers restore independent finger extension and don’t sacrifice wrist flexion power. The trade-off is 9-12 months waiting for reinnervation vs immediate function with tendon transfer.

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Mainstay for closed palsies; observe 3 months Cock-up wrist orthosis + dynamic outriggers; maintain passive ROM Radial nerve palsy alone is not an indication for surgical fixation of humeral fracture

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Tendon Transfers › Outcomes
text: Moussavi (41 pts) : all three methods successful; no ROM/DASH/RTW difference; 95% would repeat; mean RTW 4.5 months (FCR group) Ishida & Ikuta (21 pts, FCR-based, 11.3 yr) : avg wrist extension 54°, flexion 42°; MCP extension 5° with wrist at 30° extension; grip 63% contralateral; bowstringing in 12/21 (all PL→EPL)

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Radial nerve palsy with closed humeral fracture → observe 3 months; 71% recover spontaneously Open fractures + radial palsy → early exploration (lower spontaneous recovery) PT → ECRB is universal across all three transfer methods — start learning this one Don’t sacrifice FCU if you can avoid it — it’s the most powerful wrist flexor and critical for ulnar deviation PL absence (up to 20%) shifts you from FCR-based to FDS-based method Concurrent nerve transfer + tendon transfer (e.g., FDS→ECRB as “internal splint” while awaiting nerve transfer recovery) is an emerging strategy Full passive ROM mandatory before any tendon transfer

title: Radial Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Tendon Transfers › Principles (7 rules)
text: Donor must be expendable Adequate strength (loses 1 grade) Similar excursion/resting length One function per tendon Straight line of pull Synergistic (wrist flexion = finger extension; wrist extension = finger flexion) Full passive ROM at all joints before transfer

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Origin: medial cord (C8-T1); pierces medial intermuscular septum ~8 cm above medial epicondyle Arcade of Struthers : aponeurotic band from medial intermuscular septum to medial head triceps (~5.7 cm proximal to epicondyle) Only major nerve on opposite side of axis of joint rotation → vulnerable to compression + traction with flexion FCU innervation: avg 3.4 branches (Tubbs); FDP ring/small: 3 cm distal to medial epicondyle DCU branches 7 cm proximal to wrist → key localizing feature At wrist: 2 fascicular bundles — sensory (volar/ulnar) and motor (dorsal/radial) Motor distribution: hypothenar (ADM, FDM, ODM, palmaris brevis), 3 palmar + 4 dorsal interossei, lumbricals 3-4, adductor pollicis, deep head FPB Most terminal motor branches are farthest from plexus of any terminal brachial plexus branch → high injuries have worst prognosis for intrinsic recovery Interconnections: Martin-Gruber (forearm, 17%), Riche-Cannieu (hand, 77%)

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient with a high ulnar nerve laceration has less clawing than expected. Why? — A: The “ulnar paradox” — FDP to ring and small fingers is also denervated in high lesions, so the extrinsic flexors cannot overpower the extensors at the IP joints, resulting in less apparent clawing. Q: A patient with ulnar claw hand has a positive Bouvier maneuver and full passive ROM. What is the simplest surgical option? — A: Zancolli FDS lasso (dynamic, modulates with wrist position) or MCP capsulodesis (static, simpler but stretches over time). Q: Which tendon transfer restores thumb adduction in ulnar nerve palsy? — A: Smith transfer — ECRB elongated with free graft, tunneled dorsal-to-volar between long and ring metacarpals, to the adductor pollicis insertion at the ulnar thumb MCP. Q: What nerve transfer provides “anti-clawing” by restoring intrinsic function after proximal ulnar nerve injury? — A: AIN-to-motor branch of ulnar nerve (end-to-end); the “supercharge” end-to-side variation can supplement recovery from proximal repair. Q: In a complex claw hand (negative Bouvier), why must the Stiles-Bunnell FDS 4-tail pass palmar to the deep transverse metacarpal ligament? — A: To maintain the volar axis relative to the MCP joint — this ensures the transfer flexes the MCP and extends the IPs (replicating intrinsic function) rather than just flexing the digit.

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Classification
text: Low ulnar palsy (at/distal to wrist): intrinsic motor + palmar ulnar sensory loss; FCU/FDP ring-small + dorsoulnar sensation PRESERVED High ulnar palsy (proximal to DCU): adds FCU/FDP ring-small weakness + dorsoulnar sensory loss Ulnar paradox : clawing is LESS pronounced in high palsy (FDP ring-small also weakened, so extrinsic flexors can’t hyperextend MCPs as effectively)

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Ulnar nerve: worst prognosis of 3 major UE nerves — Seddon: only 31% good sensory, 13% good motor recovery High repairs far worse than low (long regeneration to intrinsics) Children < 12: 87% complete recovery; adolescents 12-20: 67% (Chemnitz) Capsulodesis: stretches over time; only 47% satisfactory clawing resolution (Brown, 44 pts) FDS 4-tail + ECRL 4-tail both correct extensor lag equally; lag > 30° improves 45%; < 30° improves 75% Smith transfer: 50% contralateral lateral pinch strength; adding index abductorplasty → 75% pinch but unacceptable index posture AIN→ulnar motor: improved pinch + grip, decreased clawing, minimal donor morbidity (PT compensates for PQ)

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Workup › Electrodiagnostics
text: Same principles as cubital tunnel; NAP across neuroma-in-continuity = 90% continued recovery

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Duchenne sign : ring/small clawing (lost intrinsic MCP flexion + lumbrical IP extension → EDC hyperextends MCP, extrinsics flex IP) Wartenberg sign : persistent small finger abduction (3rd palmar interosseous paralyzed; EDM unopposed) Froment sign : thumb IP hyperflexion during lateral pinch (lost adductor pollicis + deep FPB → FPL overpowers EPL) Pinch grip decreased 50-75% ; 75% of thumb adduction power lost “Roll-up flexion” : extrinsics flex MCPs only after IP terminal flexion → pushes objects out of palm Bouvier maneuver : passively flex MCPs → ask patient to extend IPs Positive = central slip competent → “simple” claw hand Negative = “complex” claw hand → then assess passive IP motion (flexible vs stiff) Full passive ROM required before any tendon transfer Key decision point : Bouvier test determines reconstruction strategy. Positive Bouvier = simple claw = Zancolli lasso or capsulodesis. Negative Bouvier = complex claw = Stiles-Bunnell or ECRL 4-tail to restore IP extension.

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › FDP Side-to-Side (High Ulnar Palsy)
text: Long FDS removed; FDP ring + small sutured side-to-side to FDP long FDP index left independent “Reverse cascade” tensioning — all 3 flex to palm in unison

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Repair
text: Acute laceration → primary repair; failed regeneration at 3-4 months → explore Avulsion/blast/GSW: wait 2-3 weeks for zone demarcation Resect to healthy fascicles; tension-free; epineurial suture ± fibrin glue Anterior transposition can reduce nerve gap by ~4 cm

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Nerve Transfers
text: AIN → Ulnar Motor (End-to-End) - Indicated for high ulnar injury proximal to elbow - AIN harvested at PQ; coapt to proximally transected ulnar motor fascicle - Contraindications: late presentation (> 9-12 mo), concurrent median injury Supercharge End-to-Side (SETS) - Epineurial window in ulnar motor fascicle 8-10 cm proximal to wrist; AIN sutured end-to-side - Indicated for: severe cubital tunnel, axonotmetic elbow/forearm injury, Parsonage-Turner - Supplements, doesn’t replace, recovery from proximal repair Radial → Ulnar Motor - For combined median + ulnar injury: PIN branches (EDM + ECU) → ulnar motor (Tung) Bertelli Distal Transfer - Opponens pollicis branch → terminal deep branch ulnar nerve → reinnervates FDI + adductor pollicis for pinch Sensory Transfers - Palmar median branches → ulnar digital nerve of small finger - Combined median + ulnar palsy: PIN at wrist → DCU for ulnar border sensation

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Non-operative
text: Passive ROM all affected joints Lumbrical bar splint : prevents MCP hyperextension + volar plate attenuation; maintains “simple claw” Splinting prevents progression from simple → complex claw

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Ulnar paradox: less clawing with high palsy (seems counterintuitive) — because FDP ring/small is also denervated Bouvier maneuver is the key decision point: positive → static/lasso; negative → 4-tail transfer Don’t use Stiles-Bunnell in a patient with positive Bouvier — creates iatrogenic swan neck Lumbrical bar splinting early prevents progression from simple → complex claw Riche-Cannieu anastomosis (77%) can mask ulnar motor deficits — intrinsic function may be partially preserved via median crossover Anterior transposition reduces gap by ~4 cm — consider before defaulting to graft Late presentation, failed repair, long gaps → tendon transfers; outcomes limited by scar, line-of-pull challenges

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Nerve transfers : 4 stages — acute (splint/edema/pain), early motor re-education at 3 wk (mirror therapy), strengthening once voluntary twitch, functional ADL use Capsulodesis : dorsal blocking splint MCP 60° flexion x 4 wk; thermoplastic → night splint until 8 wk Stiles-Bunnell / ECRL 4-tail : splint wrist neutral, MCP 60° flexion, IPs full extension; thermoplastic at 4 wk; free IPs at 6 wk; activities at 6-8 wk Smith transfer : splint wrist 30° extension, thumb palmar abducted x 4 wk → 4 more weeks; activities at 6 wk

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Tendon Transfers — Complex Claw (Negative Bouvier + Flexible IP)
text: Stiles-Bunnell FDS 4-Tail - Harvest FDS long + ring (low palsy) or long only (high palsy) - Split into 4 tails → insert into radial lateral bands of long/ring/small + ulnar lateral band of index - Pass palmar to deep transverse metacarpal ligament (maintains volar axis to MCP) - Tensioned: wrist neutral, MCP 60-70° flexion - Don’t use with positive Bouvier (creates swan neck) ECRL 4-Tail (Brand) - ECRL harvested at index MC base; elongated with 4 palmaris graft tails - Tunneled dorsal→volar in 2nd/3rd/4th interspaces → sutured to lateral bands - Used when FDS unavailable (combined injury) or joint hyperlaxity - More adhesion-prone due to graft interposition

title: Ulnar Nerve Injury and Tendon Transfers
heading: Treatment › Tendon Transfers — Simple Claw Hand (Positive Bouvier)
text: Zancolli MCP Capsulodesis (1957) - Static procedure; distally based volar plate flap → advanced proximally → anchored to MC neck - MCP held at 40-50° flexion; splint x 4 wk - Limitation : stretches over time → only 47% satisfactory at > 12 mo (Brown) Zancolli FDS Lasso - Dynamic; FDS divided at A3 (distal to Camper’s chiasm) → retrieved under A2 → wrapped around A1 → sutured to itself - Tensioned: wrist neutral, MCP 40° (ring), 50° (small) - High UN palsy: harvest long finger FDS, split into 2 tails → wrap ring + small A1 pulleys - Tenodesis effect modulates flexion with wrist position

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: FDS : dual origin (medial epicondyle + proximal radius); median nerve; dual blood supply (radial + ulnar arteries) FDP : IO membrane + volar ulna; ulnar artery; dual innervation — ulnar nerve (small + ring), AIN (middle + index) FPL : IO membrane + distal radius; AIN; radial artery dominant Linburg-Comstock anomaly : tendinous connection FDP-index to FPL — 31% unilateral, 16% bilateral; must recognize during exploration Carpal tunnel arrangement: FDP deepest (coronal), FPL most radial, FDS index + small deep to ring + middle Pulley system : 5 annular (A1-A5), 3 cruciate (C1-C3); A2 + A4 = critical (skeletally based); thumb equivalent = oblique pulley Vincula at cruciate pulley level — preserve during repair Healing: intrinsic pathway (epitenon → restores gliding, desired) vs extrinsic pathway (synovial sheath → adhesions)

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Biomechanical Principles
text: Strand count > caliber : 4-0 eight-strand beats 3-0 four-strand by 43% Optimal purchase: 7-10 mm; locks/grasps ≥ 2 mm Gap > 3 mm detrimental to strength accrual Suture: nylon/Supramid preferred for zone I/II; FiberWire too rigid, Ethibond too extendable

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient sustains a Zone I FDP avulsion that retracts to the palm with no bony fragment. What is the Leddy-Packer type, and what is the critical timing concern? — A: Type I; must repair urgently as vincular blood supply is disrupted by retraction past the lumbrical origin. Q: During zone II flexor tendon repair, how many core suture strands are recommended, and what gap threshold is considered detrimental? — A: ≥ 4 strands; gap > 3 mm impairs strength accrual. Q: A 4-0 eight-strand repair is compared to a 3-0 four-strand repair. Which is stronger, and by how much? — A: The 4-0 eight-strand is 43% stronger — strand count is more critical than suture caliber. Q: What is the most important intraoperative check after completing a zone II flexor tendon repair? — A: Digital extension-flexion test — confirm no gap on extension and no impingement on flexion through the pulley system. Q: Which two annular pulleys must be preserved to prevent bowstringing, and what is the maximum total length of pulley that can be safely vented? — A: A2 and A4; up to 2 cm total venting on the palmar aspect is safe.

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Classification
text: Kleinert-Verdan Zones: Zone Anatomy I Distal to FDS insertion (FDP only) II A1 to FDS insertion (“no man’s land”); Tang subzones IIa-IId III Distal TCL to proximal A1 (high NV injury rate) IV Within carpal tunnel V Forearm proximal to CT Thumb: T1-T4 mirror finger zones Leddy-Packer (Zone I FDP avulsions): I = retraction to palm; II = retraction to PIP; III = bony fragment at A4

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Dy systematic review: 6% reoperation, 4% rupture, 4% adhesions Tenolysis for limited active motion despite full passive — wait ≥ 3-6 months Re-rupture → re-repair if early; otherwise two-stage reconstruction > 3 weeks delayed : usually two-stage reconstruction needed

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Workup › Exam
text: Loss of resting cascade, absent tenodesis effect → laceration Test FPL, FDS, FDP independently; FDS to small absent ~6% NV exam first (2PD, Semmes-Weinstein, Doppler) US : 83% sens / 85% spec for high-grade zone II partial lacerations 50% rule for partials: < 50% trim edges only; > 50% repair

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Workup › History
text: Ideal repair within 7 days ; hand dominance, mechanism, position at injury Emergency only if digital blood supply compromised

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Operative — By Zone
text: Zone I: - ≥ 1 cm distal stump → direct core + epitendinous repair - < 1 cm stump → direct end-to-end with 10-12 strands of 4-0 nylon (Tang shift away from pullout button) - Bony avulsion fragment → screw, IO wire, or suture Zone II (most variable outcomes): - Standard: ≥ 4-strand repair with 3-0/4-0 braided nonabsorbable + epitendinous - M-Tang 6-strand with sparse peripheral sutures becoming preferred globally - Pulley venting ≤ 2 cm total, palmar cut — no significant bowstringing - Digital extension-flexion test intraop: no gap on extension, no impingement on flexion - FDS repair debated; only FDP in zone IIc (narrowest sheath) Zones III-V: better outcomes; mandatory NV exam; larger gauge sutures FPL: often retracts into carpal tunnel/forearm; 87% good/excellent with 6-strand M-Tang + pulley vents Barrera: OR setup sequence — antibiotics → tourniquet placed → prep/drape → local → Esmarch + inflate. Skip Esmarch exsanguination in tumor or infection cases; elevate only.

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: FDS to small finger absent in ~6% — always test individually Linburg-Comstock can cause unexpected FPL retraction when exploring FDP-index Zone IIc is the narrowest sheath — repair FDP only Gap > 3 mm at repair = detrimental; always check with intraop extension-flexion test Children: repair when possible; 4-week immobilization if non-compliant; 96% excellent outcomes (Sikora) Strand count matters more than suture caliber

title: Flexor Tendon Injuries
heading: Post-op / Rehab
text: Early active motion preferred — Trumble RCT: place-and-hold > passive (156° vs 128° TAM) Nantong protocol (Tang): - Start day 4-5; 4-6 sessions/day × 15-20 min - 10+ passive ROM cycles → 40-60 runs active flexion to half/two-thirds initial range - Half a fist; avoid extreme flexion; out-of-splint motion OK - Week 3-4: aim full active ROM - Splint: wrist neutral/slight flexion, MCP ~30° flexion Starr systematic review: active = more ruptures (5% vs 4%) BUT better ROM (6% vs 9% stiffness) WALANT: enables intraop active motion check; patient sees repair → better compliance

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Board-Style Questions (4)
text: Q: A Boyes grade III patient with joint damage and decreased ROM — is this a single-stage or two-stage reconstruction candidate? — A: Two-stage; single-stage requires Boyes grade I (good tissue, mobile joints, minimal scar). Q: During single-stage flexor tendon reconstruction, should the graft be secured distally or proximally first, and why? — A: Distal first — easier finger wound closure before the digit is flexed by proximal tensioning. Q: What complication results from a flexor tendon graft that is tensioned too tight? — A: Quadriga — the tight graft limits excursion of all FDPs (shared muscle belly), reducing adjacent digit flexion. Q: What is the ideal time window for tenolysis after flexor tendon reconstruction? — A: ≥ 3 months and ≤ 1 year post-healing, once the patient has plateaued in therapy with full passive but limited active motion.

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Classification
text: Boyes Preoperative Classification: Grade Condition Implication I Good — minimal scar, mobile joints Single-stage candidate II Notable scar, mild contracture Likely two-stage III Joint damage, decreased ROM Two-stage IV Nerve damage Two-stage V Multiple systems (II+III+IV) Two-stage

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: Tendon rupture ~7% PIP motion loss: ~30% lose ≥ 30° Need for tenolysis after reconstruction: 12-47% Quadriga : graft too tight / distal adhesions → all FDPs limited (single muscle belly) Paradoxical extension : graft too loose → lumbricals drive IP extension DIP/PIP flexion deformity (8-55°) nearly universal Wide-awake tensioning helps avoid Quadriga and paradoxical extension

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Workup › History
text: Prior repair details, timing, mechanism, hand dominance, functional demands Document TAM, TAF, TAE, DPC (active + passive) TAM “normal” = 260° (MCP included) or 175° (PIP + DIP only) Assess digital cascade with wrist flex/ext

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Workup › Imaging
text: XR for arthritis, fracture, deformity MRI/US with caution — pseudotendon can be misread as intact tendon

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Operative — Single-Stage Reconstruction
text: Indications: Intact flexor sheath + pulley system, flexible digit, failed primary repair or delayed presentation Both FDS + FDP injured → reconstruct FDP only Intact FDS + functional PIP → reconstructing FDP may do more harm (except young high-demand 10-21 yo) Pass graft via pediatric feeding tube or tendon passer Distal fixation : direct suture to remnant preferred (Tang: 10-12 strands 4-0 nylon); alternatives = pullout button, bone tunnel, screw, suture anchor Proximal : Pulvertaft weave (≥ 2-3 weaves + cross-stitching) in palm or distal forearm Secure distal first → easier wound closure before flexion Tensioning : restore digital cascade; slightly tighter (stretches over time); gradually more flexion index → small

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Operative — Two-Stage Reconstruction (Hunter)
text: Indications: Substantial sheath disruption, severe trauma/crush, failed primary repair or grafting Stage 1: - Silicone rod implant (4 mm typical) creates pseudosheath (mesothelial cell-lined) - Anchor distally to ≥ 1 cm FDP remnant if possible - Therapy: wound healing, reduce inflammation, minimal motion (excess → synovitis) - Infection rate ~15% Stage 2 (8-16 wk, later preferable): - Pull rod from distal end → pass tendon graft through pseudosheath - Slight extra tension for anticipated loosening - Pulvertaft weave proximally Modified Paneva-Holevich (preferred by some): - Stage 1: rod placed + FDS/FDP sutured as loop in palm - Stage 2: rod removed, pedicled FDS flap used as graft — no additional donor tendon needed; one side already healed WALANT preferred for flexor tendon reconstruction — enables intraop active motion assessment, real-time tensioning, and patient education Barrera: For tumor or infection cases, skip Esmarch exsanguination — elevate only.

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Workup › Patient Selection
text: ≥ 1 uncompromised digital nerve required Contraindications : NV impairment, intractable flexion contractures, noncompliance Preoperative aggressive therapy program — improves motion AND tests compliance Discuss alternatives: arthrodesis, amputation, transfer, tenodesis, no surgery

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls
text: Hierarchy: primary repair > tenolysis > single-stage graft > two-stage (final attempt) Intact FDS with functional PIP — think twice before reconstructing FDP in low-demand patients Preserve ≥ 3 pulleys for single-stage; A2 + A4 most important Modified Paneva-Holevich avoids a separate donor tendon harvest Children: wait until ≥ 6 yo; avoid bone tunnels (physis); modified Paneva-Holevich preferred

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Pulley Reconstruction
text: Indications: Severe bowstringing, multiple pulley injury, flexion lag; full passive motion via therapy first Reconstruct A2 + A4 minimum (± A3) Best graft material : extensor retinaculum (pre-existing synovial gliding surface) Harvest proximal to Lister’s tubercle (more robust) A2 reconstruction: graft under extensor tendon; A4: graft over conjoined extensor Techniques: Bunnell (1 wrap), Lister (least resistance), Karev belt-loop (strongest but decreases ROM) Avoid bone drill holes (phalangeal fracture risk) Postop: external pulley ring bolster × 4-6 weeks

title: Flexor Tendon Reconstruction
heading: Treatment › Tenolysis
text: Best ≥ 3 months and ≤ 1 year post-healing Prerequisite: full passive but limited active motion; therapy plateau Wide-awake surgery preferred (real-time active motion assessment) Results: 50-70° TAM improvement in 80% of patients; 20% no gain or loss Start therapy within first few days postop — most motion achieved in first week

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Anatomy / Basic Science
text: Extrinsic extensors form dorsal hood at MCP with sagittal bands to volar plate; centralize tendon + extend P1 Long extensor trifurcates distal to P1 → central slip (→ middle phalanx) + 2 lateral slips Lateral bands (intrinsic + lateral slips) → terminal tendon → distal phalanx Triangular ligament prevents dorsal subluxation of lateral bands; transverse retinacular ligament prevents dorsal migration at PIP ORL : present < 50%; most often ulnar side ring finger Prime MCP flexors = intrinsics (tendons volar to MCP axis, dorsal to PIP/DIP axes) Grip strength markedly decreased with extensor paralysis Quadriga concept : finger extensors function as single muscle unit — basis for relative motion splinting Wrist Compartments: # Contents Pearl 1 APL + EPB EPB separate subcompartment 35-45% 2 ECRL + ECRB 3 EPL Angles around Lister’s tubercle 4 EDC + EIP EIP deepest, shortest belly 5 EDM Usually bifid 6 ECU Always in separate subsheath EDC to small finger absent < 50% (junctura tendinum substitutes) Extensor digitorum brevis manus : aberrant muscle (PIN innervation); may be sole index extensor — do NOT excise Thumb: EPL = primary central extensor; no lumbricals/interossei; APB (radial) + adductor (ulnar) → dorsal aponeurosis → IP extension

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Board-Style Questions (5)
text: Q: A patient presents with a painful, stiff PIP joint after a dorsal laceration over the proximal phalanx. On exam, passive DIP flexion is more difficult with PIP extended than flexed. What does this indicate? — A: Boutonniere deformity (positive Boyes test) — lateral band dorsal subluxation tethers the terminal tendon with PIP extension. Q: A 30-year-old presents 2 weeks after a closed sagittal band rupture with extensor subluxation at the middle finger MCP. What is the best initial treatment? — A: Relative motion extension splint for 6 weeks — acute splinting within 3 weeks has a 95% success rate. Q: After non-displaced distal radius fracture, a patient develops inability to extend the thumb IP joint. What is the diagnosis and optimal treatment? — A: Attritional EPL rupture at Lister’s tubercle; EIP-to-EPL tendon transfer. Q: On exam, a patient has difficulty with passive PIP flexion when the MCP is extended, but PIP flexion improves with MCP flexed. Is this intrinsic or extrinsic tightness? — A: Intrinsic tightness (positive Bunnell test); extrinsic tightness shows the opposite pattern. Q: A bony mallet fracture involves 40% of the articular surface with no DIP subluxation. What is the recommended treatment? — A: DIP extension splint 24/7 for 6-8 weeks — even large bony fragments respond to splinting when the joint remains congruent.

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Complications & Outcomes
text: MCP extension contracture from prolonged splinting (most common) Bunnell test (intrinsic tightness): MCP extended → passive PIP flexion difficult vs Extrinsic tightness : MCP flexed → PIP flexion harder Tenolysis: wait ≥ 4 months; therapy must be at plateau Wong systematic review (zones IV-VII): TAM relative motion 205-236° vs dynamic 191-214° vs static 79-202°

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Pearls / Pitfalls

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone I-II — Mallet Deformity
text: Doyle Classification: I = closed ± avulsion; II = open laceration; III = open + tissue loss; IVa = pediatric physeal; IVb = 20-50% articular; IVc = > 50% + volar subluxation Closed (Type I): - DIP extension splint 24/7 × 6-8 weeks + gradual daytime weaning; leave PIP free - Even large bony fragments respond to splinting alone - Outcomes: 7.6° extensor lag, 12.8% complication rate Bony mallet with DIP subluxation: - Extension block pinning (Ishiguro) : 0.045 K-wire 45° to P2 head as block + second retrograde K-wire across DIP; remove 4-6 weeks Open (Type II/III): 5-0 monofilament tendon repair + K-wire DIP pinning Chronic mallet → swan neck: Fowler tenotomy (divide central extensor at PIP); wait ≥ 6 months; SORL reconstruction or FDS volar PIP tenodesis for fixed deformity

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone III — Central Slip / Boutonniere
text: Initial presentation may be subtle — lateral bands can extend PIP early Modified Elson test : PIP fully flexed against resistance; rigid DIP extension = positive (central slip injury) Acute closed: PIP extension splint 6-8 weeks continuous + active DIP flexion hourly; then part-time 4-6 weeks Acute open: < 50% → wound care + early motion; complete → ORIF with 4-0/5-0 + PIP pinning in extension × 5-6 weeks Chronic boutonniere: - Boyes test : passive DIP flexion harder with PIP extended (vs pseudoboutonniere) - Conservative first — serial casting/splinting → relative motion flexion splint × 3 months - Surgical outcomes unpredictable; worse with PIP fixed flexion, age > 45, prior surgery - Curtis stepwise approach : TRL release → tenolysis → central slip reinforcement

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone V — Sagittal Band Injuries
text: Closed sagittal band rupture: radial side middle/ring most common Acute (< 3 wk): relative motion extension splint × 6 weeks — 95% success (Peelman) 3 wk delay: only ~50% succeed with splinting → surgical repair Fight bite : always evaluate for MCP joint penetration; aggressive I&D + IV antibiotics + delayed closure

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone VI (Dorsum of Hand)
text: Thicker tendons; 3-0 core suture; > 80% good/excellent regardless of postop protocol Loss of MCP flexion = most frequent complication

title: Extensor Tendon Injuries
heading: Treatment › Zone VII-VIII
text: EPL rupture after non-displaced DRF → EIP-to-EPL transfer (optimal) Zone VIII: don’t wait > 4 weeks — muscle contracture becomes permanent Relative motion splinting is increasingly preferred for zones V-VI — leverages the quadriga concept, keeping the injured tendon in relative extension while permitting near-normal hand function and therapy
